The heat map's own shape makes the register's priority order visible without further arithmetic: nothing sits in the High-probability, High-impact cell, because the one structurally dangerous risk (R1, the lease rate) is judged Low probability on the strength of the verified market evidence in section 21.2, and the two Medium-probability, High-impact risks (R3 and R5) are both contract risks the sequencing decision in research section 2 was deliberately designed to survive, not eliminate. The single High-probability, Medium-impact risk, R8 rider attrition, is the one item in the register that is best read not as a risk to be mitigated away but as an operating cost to be budgeted for continuously, consistent with the industry-wide evidence in section 21.3.

21.6 Pre-mortem: it is month 12 and the plan has failed, the three most likely stories

A pre-mortem asks the question backward: assume the plan has already failed by month 12, the point at which the contract fleet should be complete at 75 vehicles and the last 10 petrol bikes should have been sold T8, and ask what story would explain it. Three stories, built directly from the risks above, are the most likely.

The first story is the contract story. The client never awards the contract, or awards it and then does not ramp volume, so by month 12 SwiftKart has completed its own electrification (waves 1 and 2, 90 leased EVs and 10 spares on the existing fleet, T8) but has no contract fleet, no contract revenue and a reporting platform built for a client relationship that did not materialise at scale. In this story the plan has not failed in the sense of losing money, the no-award branch still delivers ₹3.34 crore of NPV and ₹1.88 crore more than staying petrol T5, but it has failed against the ambition the case itself frames: pursuing the growth opportunity C O09. The lesson this story teaches is that the sequencing decision (electrify first) was the correct insurance against exactly this outcome, and that the ₹31.5 lakh committed to the charging hub and reporting platform before contract award (R3's control) should be re-examined if, by month 6, no award signal has appeared at all.

The second story is the operations story. The contract is awarded and the fleet is built on schedule, but fulfilment on the contract fleet sits persistently below the 95% floor C O03 through months 7 to 12 because charging downtime and rider attrition (R6 and R8) compound each other during the hot months (R7): a rider absence leaves a vehicle idle rather than charging on schedule, and a charging delay leaves a rider without a vehicle, each making the other worse. By month 12 the client has issued a formal service-level warning, and the ₹123.3 lakh a year of contract margin the bridge in research section 18 counts on T15 is at risk of being clawed back through contract penalties the case brief does not price but any real e-commerce contract would carry. The lesson this story teaches is that the 10-spares and two-hub-supervisor staffing in section 23 is not a cost to be trimmed under budget pressure; it is the control for the single most compounding pair of risks in the register.

The third story is the money story. The contract is awarded and runs, but the working-capital line runs hotter than the verified 57-day assumption A01, the reserve (already thinned to ₹5.8 lakh at the model's M1 update, T9) is drawn down faster than it is replenished, and by month 12 SwiftKart is closer to the ₹1,000,000 minimum cash floor A25 than the plan intended, even though the model shows the recommended plan should never actually breach that floor, lowest cash in the base case is ₹1.016 crore by month 2, far above ₹10 lakh, and the bear case still clears ₹63.0 lakh T7, T10. This story is the least likely of the three on the model's own numbers, but it is the one most within SwiftKart's own control to prevent, since it depends on a contract term (receivable days) that can be negotiated at signing rather than on a client decision or an operational condition outside SwiftKart's reach, which is exactly why R10's control is to cap receivable days in the contract itself, not to rely on the reserve to absorb an overrun after the fact.

The contract story (no award, or awarded but not ramped) R3, R4, R5 No-award branch, ₹3.34 crore NPV, ₹1.88 crore above staying petrol T5
The operations story (fulfilment below 95% through compounding charging, rider and heat risk) R6, R7, R8 Not separately modelled; the qualitative risk is contract penalty exposure the case brief does not price
The money story (working capital overrun draws down the thin reserve) R10 Base case never breaches the cash floor; bear case clears ₹63.0 lakh T7, T10

What this section establishes, and what it does not

  • Twelve risks are registered with a probability, an impact, an early signal, a trigger, a control and a named owner each, covering all seven of the case's own uncertainties [C U01 to C U07] plus five risks this document adds (lessor concentration, award timing, operational attrition, working-capital overrun and reporting non-conformance).
  • The single risk that would change the recommendation itself, the lease rate repricing above ₹5,153 a month T13, is rated Low probability on the strength of verified market evidence (Alt Mobility's ₹2,800 starting rate, RB19), not assumed away; kill criterion 1 was checked against this exact evidence and not triggered.
  • The heat map and the pre-mortem both show the contract risks (not awarded, or awarded but under-ramped) as the most consequential pair, and both are shown to leave the plan at ₹3.34 crore of NPV, not zero, because electrification was sequenced ahead of the contract rather than dependent on it.
  • This section does not quantify the heat, monsoon or reporting risks in rupee terms where no verified Delhi-specific figure exists (lane R-F's own gaps section); it states the mechanism and the absence of a number rather than inventing one.
  • This section does not revisit the scenario and sensitivity analysis itself (research section 19) or the roadmap's own gate structure (research section 22, next), which carry the quantitative and sequencing detail this register draws on.

22. The 24-month roadmap: four gates decide each next step

Answer. The 24-month roadmap runs in three waves on the existing fleet (50 EVs in month 2, 40 in month 4, the last 10 in month 12) and three tranches on the contract fleet (25 EVs each in months 4, 6 and 8), all leased, with four gates, G1 at month 3, G2 at month 8, G3 at month 12 and G4 at month 24, each testing one binary question and each carrying a defined fallback if the test fails T4, T7, T8. By month 12 the plan reaches 100 EVs on the existing fleet, 75 on the contract fleet and 10 spares with zero petrol bikes remaining T8; by month 24 the recommended plan is running at ₹206.0 lakh a year of contribution T15 with cash at ₹3.74 crore and no debt drawn at any point T5. If the contract is never awarded, the no-award branch (section 21.1, R3) still completes the existing-fleet electrification on an unchanged schedule and still delivers ₹3.34 crore of NPV T5.

22.2 Month by month through the first 12 months, where the capital actually moves

The month-by-month table in model table T7 is the roadmap's own ledger, and three things in it are worth drawing out in prose rather than leaving as numbers alone. First, the single largest investment month is month 2, at ₹22.9 lakh T7, the month wave 1 (50 EVs, 4 spares) is leased and the charging hub and lease deposits are first committed; this is also the only month in the first year where cash falls in absolute terms before recovering, from ₹103.5 lakh to ₹101.6 lakh T7, a fall of only ₹1.9 lakh because ₹15.0 lakh of petrol-bike resale proceeds C X05 land in the same month and partly offset the investment. Second, months 4, 6 and 8 each carry a working capital charge (₹10.4 lakh, ₹12.6 lakh and ₹14.8 lakh respectively, T7) as the contract's 57-day receivable cycle A01 catches up with the revenue the new contract tranches generate; this is the mechanical reason the ₹44.5 lakh working-capital line in research section 17 is the single largest use of the ₹1 crore T9, and the roadmap table makes visible exactly which months draw it down. Third, cash never falls below ₹101.6 lakh at any point in the first 24 months in the base case T7, which is ₹91.6 lakh above the ₹10 lakh minimum cash floor assumption A25, confirming the scenario finding in research section 19 that the recommended plan clears its own floor without debt in the base case and, per T10, in the bear case too.

A fourth point worth drawing out concerns the case's own task statement T02, T03, which asks the recommendation to address financial position, growth opportunity, fleet strategy, operational requirements and long-term competitive position together, not separately. The roadmap is the one artefact in this document that actually does this in a single structure: the fleet strategy (lease, never buy) and the financial position (no debt, T5) are expressed in the same wave and tranche schedule as the growth opportunity (the contract tranches) and the operational requirement (the 95% fulfilment floor, met through spares and staggered charging, section 23), and the long-term competitive position (zero petrol bikes two years ahead of Delhi's 1 April 2028 electric-only registration rule, RE35) falls out of the schedule's own month-12 completion date rather than requiring a separate initiative.

22.3 The four gates: what each tests, and both outcomes

A gate is a defined point where management asks one binary question and commits to one of two pre-agreed next steps, rather than a date that simply passes. The four gates below are built directly from the model's own assumption timing (A08, A09, A10, A11) and from the contract's own clauses C O02, C O03, C O06.

Gate Month The test If the test passes If the test fails
G1 3 Has the contract been awarded, matching or close to the base-case month 3 assumption A08? Begin the contract tranches in months 4, 6 and 8 as planned; continue wave 2 of the existing-fleet electrification on schedule If award is delayed, slide the tranche schedule to match the confirmed award date (bear case month 5, A08) without changing the total fleet size or tranche structure; wave 2 and wave 3 of the existing fleet proceed regardless, since they do not depend on the contract
G2 8 Is the contract fleet complete at 75 vehicles and is fulfilment tracking toward the 95% floor C O03 in its first full operating month? Commit the reporting platform's live monthly submission to the client on the agreed cadence; proceed to wave 3 (the last 10 petrol bikes) on schedule at month 12 If fulfilment is tracking below 95%, add spares from the existing fleet's buffer rather than the contract's own buffer first, and delay wave 3 by one quarter until the contract fleet's availability stabilises, keeping a petrol fallback in service longer as a release valve (this is the explicit reason wave 3, not waves 1 or 2, is scheduled last)
G3 12 Is the existing fleet fully electrified (0 petrol bikes) and is the contract fleet still scaling within the case's own 12-month window C O02, C O06? Move into steady-state operation (Q5 to Q8); release the reserve for discretionary use if fulfilment has been stable at or above 95% for two consecutive months If the contract has still not reached its full 75-vehicle, 95%-fulfilment state by month 12, keep wave 3's 10 petrol bikes as an active fallback past month 12 rather than selling them at the planned, falling resale value A17, A18, and extend the contract ramp window with the client under the existing agreement rather than renegotiating the fleet size
G4 24 Has the plan delivered its own targets: ₹206.0 lakh run-rate contribution, zero debt, cash above the floor in every scenario tested T5, T10? Exercise the real option at lease renewal (month 36): buy only if the lease is repriced above the ₹5,153 a month switch point T13, otherwise renew the lease on the same or better terms If the plan has materially underperformed its own targets by month 24, use the still-undrawn 11% debt line C X08 as the first recourse before considering a change to the fleet mix, since the model shows the recommended plan needs no debt in every scenario tested including bear T10

Each gate also has a named decision owner and a maximum time allowed to act once the test result is known, which the table below sets out separately from the test and outcome table above to keep that table focused on the decision logic itself.

G1 Management (Harsh Kawatra and Dayita Arora) 2 weeks Confirm or slide the contract tranche schedule; notify both lessors of the confirmed intake dates
G2 Fleet and energy manager, with the hub supervisors 1 week Add spares from the existing fleet's buffer if fulfilment is tracking below 95%; confirm or delay wave 3

22.4 The no-award branch still delivers ₹3.34 crore, explained in full

The no-award branch is not a separate plan built from scratch; it is the recommended plan with the contract tranches (months 4, 6 and 8, 25 EVs each) simply never triggered, because G1's test fails in the worst way, no award at all rather than a delayed one. Everything else in the roadmap, waves 1, 2 and 3 of the existing-fleet electrification, the depot, the two-lessor split and the spares sizing (section 23), proceeds exactly as planned, because none of it was built contingent on the contract in the first place. This is the direct operational expression of the sequencing decision in research section 2: electrify first, then grow, specifically so that a contract that does not materialise costs the plan a growth opportunity, not a stranded investment.

Under the no-award branch, the model shows the existing fleet alone reaches ₹104.7 lakh of run-rate contribution a year by month 24, against ₹42.2 lakh today, a NPV of ₹3.34 crore over 48 months, and a lowest cash point of ₹103.5 lakh, materially identical to today's starting cash because almost none of the ₹1 crore's contract-specific lines (working capital, the larger share of the reporting platform, the contract-fleet spares) are ever drawn T5, T10. The uses of the ₹1 crore that remain relevant under the no-award branch are the charging hub (₹18.5 lakh), the lease deposits on the existing fleet alone (a smaller figure than the ₹12.9 lakh base case, since that figure covers both fleets), and a reduced reporting cost covering only basic telematics rather than the full emissions and pooled-dispatch build; the remainder of the ₹1 crore stays undeployed rather than committed to a client relationship that did not form. The scenario table shows the no-award branch itself carries bear and bull cases of ₹1.55 crore and ₹4.00 crore of NPV respectively T10, a tighter range than the recommended plan's ₹1.50 crore to ₹6.80 crore T10, because without the contract there is less upside to lose but also, as section 21's pre-mortem notes, less value at stake overall.

The table below sets the recommended plan and the no-award branch side by side on the measures that differ most, making explicit how much of the plan's total value the contract itself represents.

The practical trigger for recognising the no-award branch rather than continuing to wait is stated at gate G1: if award has not happened by month 3, the plan does not pause, it slides the tranche schedule to the confirmed award date rather than holding the fleet idle; it is only if no award signal appears at all within a further, materially longer window (R3's own trigger in section 21.1 sets this at six months with no stated reason) that management should treat the no-award branch as the operating base case rather than a temporary delay, and redirect any uncommitted contract-specific capital (the undeployed share of the ₹44.5 lakh working-capital line and the ₹13.0 lakh reporting platform, T9) toward either a reserve increase or a renewed search for an alternative volume source, rather than leaving it earmarked for a contract that may never arrive.

What this section establishes, and what it does not

  • The roadmap sequences three waves on the existing fleet and three tranches on the contract fleet across 24 months, reaching 100 existing-fleet EVs, 75 contract-fleet EVs, 10 spares and zero petrol bikes by month 12 T7, T8, run-rate contribution of ₹206.0 lakh a year and cash of ₹3.74 crore by month 24 with no debt drawn T5.
  • Four gates, G1 (month 3), G2 (month 8), G3 (month 12) and G4 (month 24), each carry one binary test and two pre-agreed outcomes, built directly from the model's own assumption timing (A08 to A11) and the contract's own clauses C O02, C O03, C O06.
  • The no-award branch is shown to be the same roadmap with the contract tranches removed, not a separate plan, which is why it still delivers ₹3.34 crore of NPV rather than ₹0 T5.
  • This section does not re-derive the risk register that each gate's failure path draws on (research section 21, previous) or the operating model, staffing, lessors and depot, that makes the roadmap physically executable (research section 23, next).
  • This section does not revisit the scenario ranges behind the gate tests (bear, base, bull), which are developed fully in research section 19.

23. Operating model: two lessors, ten spares, one depot and pooled dispatch keep fulfilment at 95%

Answer. We split the leased fleet across two named providers, Zypp Electric and Alt Mobility, hire and train 75 contract riders in three intakes matching the tranche schedule, run both fleets from one depot with staggered charging windows and 10 spares, and pool dispatch across the existing and contract clients so that neither client's demand swings alone determine fulfilment against the 95% floor C O03. No single part of this model is unverified invention: the two-lessor split answers risk R2 (section 21), the spares figure answers the 95% to 99% availability range lane R-F found for Indian delivery fleets RF14, and the pooled-dispatch rationale is reported honestly as an association drawn from adjacent vendor evidence, not as a measured result, because no pooled-dispatch-specific productivity study exists in the public domain RF61.

23.1 Riders: hiring in three intakes, training before the first shift

The contract needs 75 riders, hired in three intakes of 25 each, matching the three vehicle tranches (months 4, 6 and 8, section 22.1), rather than all at once, so that onboarding capacity is not overwhelmed and so that each intake's training can draw lessons from the one before it. The existing fleet's 100 riders are not newly hired; they are retrained on EV handling, charging discipline and battery safety as their petrol bikes convert in waves 1 and 2, a half-day course the model prices at ₹1,500 a rider in the base case (A04). New contract riders go through a fuller onboarding: police verification, training, kit and first-month insurance, priced at ₹5,000 a rider in the base case (A03), a figure this document reports as a modelling estimate, not a single verified source figure, since no Indian delivery platform's own itemised breakdown covering exactly this combination was found in lane R-F's search RF28. The lane did find the individual pieces that make up a plausible range: Shadowfax deducts a mandatory ₹1,000 onboarding fee from a rider's own earnings rather than bearing it as a cost itself RF25, life cover under the Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana costs about ₹330 to ₹400 a year RF31, and a basic delivery kit's wholesale helmet cost alone runs to roughly ₹710 to ₹1,000 a unit before tax RF35; none of these pieces individually contradicts the ₹5,000 base case, so A03 is kept unchanged under the model's own update rule (research section 4.4 of the plan).

Intake Month Riders Covers Training content
Existing-fleet retraining, group 1 2 50 (existing riders) Wave 1 Half-day course: EV handling, charging discipline, battery safety (A04)
Existing-fleet retraining, group 2 4 40 (existing riders) Wave 2 Same half-day course
Contract intake 1 4 25 (new riders) Tranche 1 Full onboarding (police verification, training, kit, first-month insurance) plus the EV course
Contract intake 2 6 25 (new riders) Tranche 2 Same full onboarding
Contract intake 3 8 25 (new riders) Tranche 3 Same full onboarding
Existing-fleet retraining, group 3 12 10 (existing riders) Wave 3 Same half-day course, the last petrol-to-EV conversion

Rider retention is treated as a recurring operating cost, not a one-time hiring programme, because the evidence from both national platforms and sector surveys is unambiguous that continuous replacement is the industry norm: Zomato's own chief executive states the company replaces roughly 1.5 lakh to 2 lakh delivery workers a month nationally RF38, and TeamLease's own employer survey names attrition the top-ranked workforce challenge in quick commerce, cited by 31% of employers surveyed RF36. SwiftKart's own 175-vehicle scale is far smaller than the national platforms these figures describe, but the direction of the evidence, that onboarding must be a standing process rather than a single event, is the operational lesson this document draws from it (also the control for risk R8, section 21.3). A fast, well-run onboarding process is linked, without a precise conversion figure, to lower early churn: the same TeamLease report states that onboarding delays of even a few days can directly raise churn risk among new hires RF37. SwiftKart's own control is therefore to complete each intake's full onboarding inside the two-month gap between tranches (months 4 to 6, 6 to 8), never letting a vehicle sit idle for want of a trained rider.

The pieces lane R-F gathered on onboarding cost, none individually matching A03's full scope, are collected below to show exactly how the ₹5,000 base-case figure was cross-checked rather than invented.

Component Evidence found Status
Police verification Non-Delhi, non-driver-specific fragments only (Kerala about ₹1,000, Andhra Pradesh receipt ₹1,000) RF28 Directional only, not a verified Delhi-rider figure
Life insurance (PMJJBY) About ₹330 to ₹400 a year for a ₹2 lakh renewable cover RF31 Verified, but a scheme a rider can self-enrol in, not necessarily an operator cost
Accident insurance (PMSBY) Roughly ₹20 a year (seen via search summary only) RF32 Snippet, not independently opened
Delivery kit (helmet) Wholesale helmet about ₹710 to ₹1,000 a unit before tax RF35 Vendor wholesale listing, not a confirmed platform purchase price
Combined itemised figure matching A03's exact scope Not found for any named Indian delivery platform RF28 Logged as a gap; A03 kept at its base-case ₹5,000 under the model's own update rule

23.2 Lessor selection: why two, and why these two

The recommended plan leases every vehicle (research section 2), which makes lessor selection the single most operationally consequential sourcing decision in the plan. We recommend splitting the fleet across two named providers rather than one, with neither holding more than 60% of either fleet, for the reason developed as risk R2 in section 21.1: a single-lessor plan concentrates service, battery-swap and insolvency risk on one counterparty for a 175-vehicle fleet the ₹1 crore partly depends on running reliably.

The two providers we recommend are Zypp Electric and Alt Mobility, chosen because their disclosed profiles are complementary rather than overlapping. Zypp Electric is the larger, delivery-focused operator of the two: its FY26 delivery-segment revenue alone was ₹322.4 crore, roughly flat on ₹323.1 crore in FY25 RB05, and its overall EV rental revenue grew 24% to ₹137.7 crore in the same year RB02, while its net loss narrowed by about 44% to ₹59.7 crore RB03, evidence of a business scaling toward, not away from, sustainability, though still loss-making, which is itself the direct basis for treating lessor concentration (R2) as a real, not theoretical, risk. Zypp's own battery-swapping expense rose 40.3% to ₹24 crore in the same year RB04, consistent with a fleet that relies on swap infrastructure (via its Indofast Energy partnership, which runs more than 670 swap stations across over 20 cities handling over one million swaps a month as of a February 2025 report [RB08a]) rather than depot-only charging, which is useful operational diversity against SwiftKart's own depot charging (section 23.3).

Alt Mobility, an IIT Delhi-founded B2B EV fleet leasing company, offers the complementary product: its FleetLease product bundles the full cost of a brand-new vehicle, no down payment, road tax, registration, comprehensive insurance, OEM-backed servicing and roadside assistance, into one lease with a typical 3- to 5-year tenure, and buy, extend or return options at the end of the term RB20. Alt Mobility's own publicly stated starting rate of ₹2,800 a month RB19 is the single most directly relevant market data point against the case's ₹3,500 lease figure C D12 and the model's ₹5,153 switch point T13, since it is well below both, which is the verified evidence behind R1's Low probability rating in section 21.2. Alt Mobility has also leased at scale before: it supplied 15,000 electric two-wheelers to Zypp Electric itself in a 2022 deal explicitly framed as keeping Zypp asset-light RB21, demonstrating that a lessor-to-lessor relationship already exists in this market, a precedent for SwiftKart leasing from one or both without being locked into either.

Dimension Zypp Electric Alt Mobility
Role in the split Majority share, both fleets; swap-network access via Indofast Energy Minority share, both fleets; buy/extend/return optionality at term end
FY26 scale evidence ₹322.4 crore delivery revenue RB05; ₹137.7 crore rental revenue, up 24% RB02 Not separately disclosed at this granularity in the sources found; AUM reported at $12 million as of a Jan 2024 round RB23
What the lease includes Vehicle, running cost, maintenance, battery access via swap network Vehicle, no down payment, road tax, registration, insurance, OEM-backed servicing, roadside assistance RB20
Typical term Not separately disclosed; the case's own 3-year term C D13 is used as the modelling basis 3 to 5 years, with buy, extend or return options RB20
Rate evidence found No single public all-in B2B rate found; the case's ₹3,500 a month C D12 is kept as the case fact per golden rule 5 Starting at ₹2,800 a month (2023 article, scope of inclusions not fully confirmed) RB19
Why this lessor is in the split Scale and delivery-sector focus reduce onboarding friction for a 175-vehicle intake The buy/extend/return option at term end is the operational route to exercising the real option at month 36 (research section 20)

Table note: lane R-B's own gaps section states plainly that no public B2B all-in monthly lease quote (vehicle, battery, swaps, maintenance and insurance together, the way the case frames its ₹3,500 figure) was found from either provider or any other named lessor; the case's own ₹3,500 figure C D12 is therefore kept as the model's base case throughout, per golden rule 5, and Alt Mobility's ₹2,800 starting rate RB19 and the case figure are reported together as directional market context, not as a substitute for the case number.

We recommend an indicative 60:40 split between Zypp Electric and Alt Mobility, by vehicle count on both fleets, rather than a fixed rupee allocation, so that the step-in clause in R2's control (section 21.1) can rebalance the split toward whichever lessor is performing better on service response without renegotiating a contract structure. This split is a modelling choice, stated as such, not a verified industry-standard ratio, since lane R-B found no published benchmark for how a 100-to-200-vehicle delivery fleet typically splits its leasing across providers.

23.3 The depot: one hub, staggered charging, sized for 175 vehicles and 10 spares

A single depot serves both fleets, sized for the full 185-unit build (100 existing EVs, 75 contract EVs, 10 spares, T8) once wave 3 and tranche 3 complete at month 12. The case's own charging infrastructure figure, ₹10 lakh for a 100-EV fleet C X01, scales to ₹18.5 lakh for the full 185-unit build in the model's uses-of-capital table T9, a proportional scale-up the model applies directly rather than independently re-deriving, since the case gives no per-unit charging cost to recompute from first principles.

The depot's layout follows directly from the charging-capacity constraint established in research section 11: a fully charged EV supports about 30 deliveries a working day C X02, which at 100% contract utilisation [O07] is exactly one full day's work with no headroom, while the existing fleet's 85% utilisation C D08 keeps roughly 15% of a charge in reserve against battery wear. The practical depot response to this zero-headroom finding is to stagger charging across the working day's shift windows rather than charge the whole fleet overnight in one block, so that a charging-related delay on one group of vehicles does not remove the whole fleet's capacity at once. We recommend three staggered charging windows, each covering no more than one third of the fleet at a time, timed against the delivery day's own demand pattern (early morning, midday and evening), so that spare capacity is always available in two of the three windows.

Depot zone Function Capacity sized for Staffing
Charging bays, window 1 Early-morning charge for the overnight-idle third of the fleet Up to roughly 62 vehicles (one third of 185) 1 hub supervisor on shift
Charging bays, window 2 Midday charge for riders between delivery peaks Up to roughly 62 vehicles Shared with window 1's supervisor on overlap
Charging bays, window 3 Evening charge ahead of the next day's early window Up to roughly 62 vehicles 1 hub supervisor on shift
Spares bay Holds the 10 spare EVs (4 existing-fleet, 6 contract-fleet by month 8, T8) ready to deploy within the depot's own turnaround time 10 vehicles Shared across both supervisors
Rider check-in and kit store Daily rider check-in, helmet and kit issue, first-aid and heat-season supplies (per RF20's advice to budget for reduced range in summer) Full rider roster across both fleets Shared across both supervisors

The depot's two-supervisor, one-fleet-and-energy-manager, one-reporting-analyst staffing (A07, ₹1.5 lakh a month base case contract operations overhead) is a modelling estimate consistent with a single-site operation of this scale; lane R-F's evidence on preventive maintenance (structured programmes associated with 15% to 25% higher availability and 40% to 60% less unplanned downtime than unstructured ones, vendor-reported, RF15) is the operational justification for staffing the depot with dedicated supervisors rather than running maintenance reactively through the lessors alone.

23.4 Dispatch pooling across two clients: an 11-point utilisation gain, reported as an association, not proof

Pooled dispatch means routing the existing fleet's quick-commerce and e-commerce clients and the new contract's deliveries through one shared rider and vehicle pool, rather than operating two separate dispatch systems, so that a demand surge on one client's volume can draw on the other client's spare capacity. This is the direct operational mechanism behind risk R5's control in section 21.2: pooled capacity cushions a single-client volume shock that a client-siloed dispatch system could not absorb without idling vehicles on one side while the other runs short.

No pooled-dispatch-specific productivity study for Indian last-mile delivery was found in lane R-F's search; every figure gathered concerns single-client route optimisation or address-matching software, a finding the lane states as its own central conclusion on this topic RF61. The adjacent evidence found is nonetheless directionally useful, reported here explicitly as an association, never as proof. One vendor's own modelled illustration finds that two last-mile fleets each running at a 61% utilisation ceiling individually can pool to a combined ceiling near 72% if their demand peaks do not coincide, an 11 percentage point gain the vendor attributes to a pooled peak-to-average ratio of about 1.18 against 1.4 for each fleet alone RF10; this is a vendor's modelled example, not a measured deployment, and is not India-specific, but it is the one figure found in this pass that speaks directly to a multi-client pooling effect rather than a single-client routing effect. Separately, high-performing Indian delivery fleets are reported to target about 85% utilisation against 60% to 70% for commercial fleets generally RF08, and a different vendor's own ceiling methodology puts an achievable utilisation ceiling at 61% for a typical last-mile parcel fleet (1.4 peak-to-average ratio) RF09, two vendor framings of the same kind of fleet that do not reconcile with each other, a disagreement this document states rather than resolves (conflict C-F3, lane R-F).

What pooled dispatch is claimed to do Evidence found How it is used in this document
Raise the combined utilisation ceiling of two fleets with non-coincident demand peaks One vendor's modelled illustration, 61% individually to about 72% pooled, an 11-point gain RF10 Reported as an association supporting the rationale for pooling, not as a measured SwiftKart result
Reduce empty-fleet distance and idle time A route-optimisation vendor's blog figures (20% to 30% empty distance, 2 to 3 hours idle time in an 8-hour shift) RF53 Reported as single-client routing evidence, explicitly not pooled-dispatch-specific
Improve fleet utilisation from a 60% to 65% baseline to 80% to 85% The same vendor's illustrative fleet-sizing example (42 to 45 vehicles instead of 50 for equivalent volume) RF55 Reported as illustrative, vendor-framed as "might require", not a named deployment result

The practical reason to pool dispatch regardless of the productivity evidence gap is structural, not statistical: the existing fleet and the contract fleet share the same depot, the same two lessors and, for riders retrained rather than newly hired, overlapping personnel, so running two separate dispatch systems would duplicate coordination effort for no operational benefit even before any pooling productivity gain is counted. The reporting and dispatch platform's own ₹13.0 lakh build cost T9 already assumes one shared system, not two, which is the honest reason the platform's cost estimate (A05) also carries no verified vendor quote matching its full scope, since no vendor found in lane R-F's search prices a combined telematics, GHG Protocol emissions reporting and pooled-dispatch system as a single product RF50.

23.5 RACI for the roadmap's four gates: who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed

Responsible means the role that does the work the gate decision requires; Accountable means the single role who owns the decision and answers for it; Consulted means a role whose input is sought before the decision is made, with a two-way exchange; Informed means a role who is told the decision after it is made, with a one-way notification. Applying these four letters consistently across the roadmap's four gates (section 22.3) makes clear that no gate is decided by the fleet and energy manager or the hub supervisors alone, even though they carry out most of the operational work the gates depend on.

Gate Responsible Accountable Consulted Informed
G1 (month 3, contract award) Fleet and energy manager (tracks award signal, prepares tranche schedule) Management (Harsh Kawatra and Dayita Arora) Finance head (working capital timing), both lessors (intake capacity) Hub supervisors, reporting analyst, all riders scheduled for upcoming intakes
G2 (month 8, fulfilment check) Hub supervisors (daily fulfilment and availability data) Fleet and energy manager Reporting analyst (data quality), the client (service-level standing) Management, finance head
G3 (month 12, full electrification) Fleet and energy manager (confirms zero petrol bikes, fleet complete) Management Finance head (reserve release decision), hub supervisors (fulfilment trend) Both lessors, reporting analyst
G4 (month 24, lease renewal real option) Finance head (prices the renewal quote against the switch point) Finance head Management, fleet and energy manager (operational continuity) Both lessors, reporting analyst

Exhibit for the deck: S5 (Recommendation and Roadmap), the roadmap and gates panels draw on this section's rider, lessor, depot and RACI detail even though the RACI table itself is not separately rendered on the slide; S6 annexure carries the fuller operating detail if space allows.

What this section establishes, and what it does not

  • Riders are hired and trained in three intakes matching the three contract tranches, with existing riders retrained rather than replaced; onboarding is treated as a continuous, not one-time, process, consistent with the industry-wide attrition evidence in lane R-F RF36, RF38.
  • The fleet is split across two named lessors, Zypp Electric and Alt Mobility, at an indicative 60:40 ratio, chosen for complementary profiles (scale and swap-network access against bundled servicing and buy/extend/return optionality) rather than a single-supplier dependency, directly answering risk R2 from research section 21.
  • The depot is sized for the full 185-unit build with staggered, three-window charging and 10 spares, a design response to the zero-headroom finding in research section 11, not an arbitrary layout choice.
  • Pooled dispatch across clients is recommended on structural grounds (shared depot, lessors and riders) and reported as supported by adjacent vendor evidence, explicitly stated as an association, not proof, since lane R-F found no pooled-dispatch-specific productivity study for Indian last-mile delivery.
  • The RACI table expands all four letters in prose once, as required, and applies them to the roadmap's own four gates rather than to a generic organisation chart.
  • This section does not price the depot, rider or lessor choices into a separate model line beyond what research section 17 (uses of the ₹1 crore) and model table T9 already carry; it explains how those rupee figures are spent operationally, not a new financial calculation.

24. KPIs and the monthly report: 14 numbers management and the client see every month

Answer. We track 14 KPIs each month, built down from contribution in a single tree (financial, operational and emissions branches), each with a stated definition, formula, data source, cadence, owner, target and trigger threshold, and we structure the client's own monthly emissions report around the six required elements ISO 14083 and the GLEC Framework define for a conformant transport-emissions report RG37, a cadence that exceeds, not merely matches, the standard's own minimum annual requirement RG45. The title above carries 14 rather than the plan's own placeholder count because that is the number of KPIs the tree below actually resolves to once the financial, operational and emissions branches are each built out with a sensible number of distinct, non-duplicate measures; this is noted here as the one titled-number discrepancy this writer found against the plan's own draft wording, logged honestly rather than forced to match a draft figure that this document's own KPI tree does not produce.

24.1 One KPI tree, three branches, resolving to the 14 numbers management tracks

A KPI tree starts from the single number that matters most, here contribution T2, T15, and decomposes it into the measures management can actually act on day to day, rather than listing KPIs as an unordered collection. The tree below has three branches: financial (what contribution is made of), operational (what drives fulfilment and availability), and emissions (what the contract clause O05 requires reported).

Branch 2 Fulfilment rate, EV availability, spares deployed Operational
Branch 2 Rider attrition, onboarding cycle time Operational
Branch 3 Grams CO2 a delivery, tonnes CO2 a year, Scope 1 and Scope 2 split Emissions

24.3 Why 14, not a round number: how the tree resolves

The title's own number, 14, is not a round target picked for the headline; it is the count that falls out of building the tree in section 24.1 to a sensible level of granularity, one KPI a distinct, actionable measure, rather than splitting any single measure into sub-metrics that would not change a decision on their own. The financial branch carries 7 KPIs (numbers 1 to 7 above), because contribution's own formula T2 has exactly that many distinct input lines once vehicle cost, rider pay, revenue per delivery, deliveries a day, utilisation and the reporting cost line are each tracked separately, consistent with the bridge structure in research section 18. The operational branch carries 5 KPIs (numbers 8 to 12), one for each distinct driver of the 95% fulfilment floor identified in research sections 11 and 21 (availability, spares, fulfilment itself, attrition, onboarding speed). The emissions branch carries 2 KPIs (numbers 13 and 14), the minimum the GLEC Framework's own "strongly recommended" disaggregation (breakdown of emissions by energy carrier, RG40) calls for: an intensity figure and a carrier split, without further splitting by mode, since SwiftKart runs one transport mode (two-wheeler) across both fleets, which makes the mode-level disaggregation ISO 14083 asks for at the required-elements level RG37 trivially satisfied by a single row rather than a separate KPI.

The table below shows the same 14 KPIs read at three points in time, today (month 0, before any conversion), month 12 (full electrification, contract fleet complete) and month 24 (steady state), so that the KPI tree is not only a specification of what to track but also a direct check against the model's own progression.

Table note: the month-12 deliveries-a-day figure is derived from model table T7's own month-12 revenue line (₹49.9 lakh) divided by the ₹40 revenue per delivery C D02 and the 26 working days a month C D04, an arithmetic check shown once here rather than repeated; it is not a separately modelled KPI output.

Reporting cadence is monthly for every KPI in the table, but the review cadence that acts on the numbers is not uniform: financial KPIs (1 to 7) are reviewed monthly by the finance head against the quarterly plan in model table T8; operational KPIs (8 to 12) are reviewed weekly by the hub supervisors internally, with only the monthly aggregate going to management and the client, so that a fulfilment dip is caught and corrected inside the same month rather than only visible after the fact; and emissions KPIs (13, 14) are reviewed monthly, matching the contract's own cadence exactly, since there is no operational reason to review them more often than they are reported. This three-speed review structure is the practical answer to the plan's own instruction that management see 14 numbers a month: management sees all 14 every month, but only two of the five operational KPIs' underlying weekly detail, since the weekly data exists to let the hub supervisors act faster than a monthly cycle would allow, not to add a second reporting burden on management itself.

Escalation step Who is informed When it triggers
Step 1, operational correction Hub supervisors act directly, no escalation Any KPI inside its normal monthly range
Step 2, management notification Fleet and energy manager informs management Any single KPI crosses its trigger threshold (section 24.2) for one month
Step 3, client notification Reporting analyst, with management's sign-off, informs the client Fulfilment rate (KPI 8) below 95% for one month, or an emissions reporting data-quality issue (KPI 13 or 14)
Step 4, gate review Management convenes the relevant roadmap gate (research section 22) ahead of schedule Two or more KPIs breach their trigger threshold in the same month, or one KPI breaches it for two consecutive months

24.4 The monthly client emissions report: layout, built to the six ISO 14083 required elements

The contract's own clause C O05 asks for monthly reporting of emissions-related metrics without specifying a format, which leaves SwiftKart free to choose a standard to report against; we recommend building the report to the ISO 14083 and GLEC Framework's own required-element list [RG37 to RG39], both because it is the named logistics-sector standard lane R-H confirmed sits one step removed from the GHG Protocol's own primary text (research section 12) and because doing so from the first report avoids the non-conformance risk (R12, section 21.4) of a format that looks complete to SwiftKart but is missing an element the client, or a future auditor, expects.

Report section ISO 14083 or GLEC element it satisfies Content
1. Transport chains covered Identification of transport chains or services (required, RG37) Named client, service type (last-mile two-wheeler delivery), reporting period
2. Total emissions Total GHG emissions (required, RG37) Tonnes CO2 for the month, Scope 1 plus Scope 2, from model table T14's method
3. Emission intensity Total GHG emission intensity, activity-distance type stated (required, RG37) Grams CO2 a delivery (KPI 13), with the distance basis (per delivery, not per kilometre) stated explicitly
4. Per-mode breakdown Total emissions and intensity for each transport mode (required, RG37) A single row, since SwiftKart runs one mode; stated as such, not omitted
5. Data quality and deviation Report frequency, data quality (primary against secondary, modelled against default), and any process deviation (required, RG38, RG39) Monthly cadence stated as exceeding the standard's annual minimum RG45; petrol and grid factors disclosed as default values from named primary sources (A21, A24)
6. Supporting information reference Reference to the location of supporting information (required, RG37) Pointer to the underlying raw telematics and dispatch data, held on the reporting platform

The report's data-quality disclosure (section 3 of the table) is the element most exposed to the non-conformance risk flagged in section 21.4: the GLEC Framework's own warning that the most common reporting error is substituting a tank-to-wheel factor where a well-to-wheel factor is required RG44 means the reporting analyst's monthly task includes confirming that the petrol emission factor used (2.31 kilograms CO2 a litre, the IPCC 2006 default, A21) and the grid factor used (0.727 kilograms CO2 a kilowatt-hour, the CEA weighted-average factor, A24) are both applied on the well-to-wheel, not tank-to-wheel, basis each source itself defines, a check this document recommends be logged explicitly inside section 5 of the monthly report rather than assumed silently.

Exhibit for the deck: S5 (Recommendation and Roadmap), the KPI table (today, month 12, month 24); S4 uses the data and dispatch line item this section's reporting cost KPI feeds.

What this section establishes, and what it does not

  • The KPI tree resolves to 14 distinct KPIs across three branches, financial (7), operational (5) and emissions (2), each built down from contribution T2, T15 rather than listed as an unordered set; this document notes honestly that 14, not a placeholder figure, is the number the tree itself produces.
  • Each of the 14 KPIs carries a definition, formula, data source, cadence, owner, target and trigger threshold, meeting the full specification the plan's own outline calls for.
  • The monthly client report is built to the six required elements of ISO 14083 and the GLEC Framework [RG37 to RG39], a cadence that exceeds the standard's own annual minimum RG45, directly answering the contract's own monthly reporting clause C O05 with a named standard rather than an invented format.
  • This section does not re-derive the emissions method itself (petrol and grid factors, the well-to-wheel arithmetic), which research section 12 covers in full; it uses those figures as KPI inputs.
  • This section does not quantify a financial penalty for missing a KPI's trigger threshold, since the case brief gives no penalty schedule for the contract; triggers are stated as management action points, not contractual break clauses.

25. Impact: 88% more deliveries, 56% less CO2 per delivery and 4.9 times the contribution

Answer. By month 24 the recommended plan runs 124,800 deliveries a month against 66,300 today, an 88% increase T14, at 106 grams of CO2 a delivery against 240 today, a 56% cut T14, while contribution rises from ₹42.2 lakh to ₹206.0 lakh a year, 4.9 times today's figure, with zero debt drawn at any point T5, T15. These three numbers are not three separate achievements; they are one plan read through three lenses, people (175 riders trained and onboarded against today's 100), planet (158.9 tonnes of CO2 a year against 190.8 today, a 17% absolute cut even as volume grows 88%, T14) and profit (NPV of ₹5.76 crore, the highest of six options modelled, T5), and all three move together because they were never separately optimised.

The table below reads all six modelled options side by side on the three lenses together, showing that the recommended plan (option 6) is not merely the best on one lens but is never worse than second-best on any of the three, which is the quantitative reason this section treats people, planet and profit as one plan rather than three separate trade-offs.

1, stay petrol 1.45 240 0
2, electrify the existing fleet by buying, no contract 2.94 114 0
3, buy for the contract, keep petrol on the existing fleet 3.36 173 35
4, buy for both fleets 4.66 106 110
5, lease for the contract, keep petrol on the existing fleet 3.80 173 0
6, lease for both fleets, electrify first (recommended) 5.76 106 0

Table note: option numbering here follows the document's own convention (option 1 to option 6, per the writer brief), matching model table T5's rows O0 to O5 in the same order; emissions figures are read directly from model table T5's own "g CO2 per delivery M24" column, not separately recalculated for this section; the no-award branch (T5 row O6, NPV ₹3.34 crore, 114 g CO2 a delivery) is option 6 without the contract tranches and is reported separately in research sections 21 and 22, not as a seventh row here.

25.1 People: 175 riders, trained before deployment, onboarded as a continuous process

The plan takes SwiftKart from 100 riders to 175 by month 8 T8, every one of them trained on EV handling, charging discipline and battery safety before their first EV shift (section 23.1), not after. The 75 new contract riders go through a fuller onboarding, police verification, training, kit and first-month insurance, priced at ₹5,000 a rider in the base case A03, a safety and welfare standard built into the model's own cost structure rather than treated as an optional extra once the contract is won. This matters because the evidence gathered in lane R-F on gig-delivery working conditions in Delhi is specific and troubling on exactly the points a 175-rider operation needs to get right: delivery workers in Delhi have reported fainting from heat during a delivery RF68, an electric three-wheeler rider in South Delhi has described waiting up to an hour longer than normal in summer to get enough charge to continue working RF65, and several workers interviewed by WRI India were penalised by their platforms for delays the source attributes to heat, meaning the cost of a heat-related delay currently falls on the rider's own pay rather than being absorbed by the platform RF67.

The plan does not claim to solve the structural conditions of gig delivery work in Delhi, which are set by the wider platform economy, not by SwiftKart's own 175-vehicle fleet; it claims something narrower and verifiable: a trained rider on a vehicle with a staggered-charging depot and 10 spares behind it (section 23.3) is less exposed to the specific failure mode lane R-F documents, a vehicle that cannot charge fast enough in the heat, than a rider without that support. Rider attrition itself is budgeted as a recurring cost, not an unplanned one, because the national evidence is unambiguous that continuous replacement is the industry norm: Zomato's own chief executive states the company replaces about 1.5 lakh to 2 lakh delivery workers a month nationally RF38, and TeamLease's own employer survey names attrition the single most-cited workforce challenge in quick commerce, named by 31% of employers surveyed RF36. Budgeting for this reality, rather than assuming it away, is itself a people-impact choice: a company that prices continuous onboarding into its model is less likely to let fulfilment slip when a rider leaves than one that treats each departure as an unbudgeted shock.

People measure Today Month 24 Source
Total riders 100 175 T8
Riders fully trained on EV handling, charging and battery safety before deployment 0 (petrol fleet) 175 (100 retrained, 75 newly onboarded) Section 23.1
Contract riders with full onboarding (verification, training, kit, insurance) 0 75 A03, section 23.1
Onboarding treated as continuous, not one-time No (not applicable, no contract) Yes, budgeted as a recurring cost RF36, RF38

25.2 Planet: emissions per delivery fall 56%, and absolute emissions fall even as volume rises 88%

The emissions result is the plan's clearest single number, and it is worth stating both ways, per delivery and in total, because a reader could otherwise mistake a falling intensity figure for proof that total emissions have risen along with volume, which is not what the model shows. Grams of CO2 a delivery fall from 240 today to 106 by month 24, a cut of (240 − 106) ÷ 240 = 55.8%, rounded to 56% T14. Over the same period, monthly deliveries rise from 66,300 to 124,800, an increase of (124,800 − 66,300) ÷ 66,300 = 88.2%, rounded to 88% T14. Multiplying intensity by volume gives the absolute result: tonnes of CO2 a year fall from 190.8 to 158.9, a cut of (190.8 − 158.9) ÷ 190.8 = 16.7%, rounded to 17%, even though volume rose 88% in the same period T14. This is the arithmetic result of electrification outrunning growth: every delivery on the contract fleet from month 8 onward and every delivery on the existing fleet from month 12 onward runs on the grid factor of 0.727 kilograms CO2 a kilowatt-hour A24, verified exactly against the Central Electricity Authority's own primary database [research section 12], rather than on the petrol factor of 2.31 kilograms CO2 a litre A21, the IPCC 2006 default.

Planet measure Today Month 24 Change Source
Grams CO2 a delivery 240 106 −56% T14
Deliveries a month 66,300 1,24,800 +88% T14
Tonnes CO2 a year 190.8 158.9 −17% T14
Petrol bikes in the fleet 100 0 −100% T8
Scope 1 emissions share 100% 0% −100 percentage points T8, section 24.2

This result exceeds, not merely matches, the contract's own clause asking for a significant proportion of deliveries on low-emission vehicles C O04: by month 24, 100% of deliveries on both fleets run on electric vehicles, not merely a significant proportion. It also arrives ahead of Delhi's own regulatory clock: new petrol two-wheeler registrations in the city become impermissible from 1 April 2028 RE35, RE41, and the Delhi Motor Vehicle Aggregator and Delivery Service Provider Scheme 2023 requires covered fleets to be fully electrified by 1 April 2030 for four-wheelers (and within four years of notification for two- and three-wheelers) RE45; SwiftKart's own fleet reaches zero petrol bikes by month 12, between 16 and 18 months ahead of the earliest of these dates. The bull-case Scope 2 opportunity lane R-G identifies, buying green power under Delhi's Green Energy Open Access regulations once the depot's sanctioned charging load approaches 100 kilowatts RG51, RG66, is not counted in the 158.9-tonne figure above, which uses the standard grid factor throughout; it is reported here as an honest upside not yet modelled, consistent with the scenario discipline the rest of this document applies to every uncertain input.

25.3 Profit: contribution rises 4.9 times, and the NPV gain is the highest of six options tested

Contribution rises from ₹42.2 lakh a year today to ₹206.0 lakh a year by month 24, a factor of 206.0 ÷ 42.2 = 4.88, rounded to 4.9 times T15. The bridge behind this number, developed in full in research section 18, attributes the rise to four moves: converting the existing fleet from petrol to lease adds ₹66.0 lakh a year (net of ₹1.7 lakh of spares cost), the contract fleet adds ₹123.3 lakh a year (net of ₹2.5 lakh of spares cost), and contract overhead and reporting running costs together subtract ₹21.3 lakh a year, netting to the ₹206.0 lakh run-rate T15. None of this rise requires debt: the recommended plan draws ₹0 of bank debt in the base case and in every scenario tested, bear and bull alike T10, which is itself a profit-quality point, not merely a liquidity one, since every rupee of the ₹163.8 lakh a year contribution gain accrues to SwiftKart without an interest cost attached.

The scorecard built in research section 13 reaches the same conclusion from a different direction: across value, liquidity, resilience, emissions and growth, weighted 0.35, 0.20, 0.20, 0.15 and 0.10 respectively, the recommended plan scores 5.00 out of 5, the maximum possible and the highest of the six options modelled, against 3.65 for buying both fleets and 1.95 for staying petrol T6. A reader who checked only the profit lens in isolation, or only the planet lens, or only the people lens, would find each one independently strong; the scorecard's own weighting shows that no single lens is doing the work alone, which is the direct evidence that these three measures were produced by one coherent plan, not assembled after the fact from three separately optimised initiatives.

The table below closes the loop back to the case's own judging criteria C I08, showing where each criterion is evidenced inside this impact section specifically, as distinct from where it is evidenced across the document as a whole (research section 1's requirements traceability matrix carries the full mapping).

Judging criterion C I08 Evidenced in this section by
Understanding Reading grams a delivery and tonnes a year together, so growth and intensity are never confused (section 25.2)
Creativity The people, planet, profit framing applied as one plan, not three separately pitched initiatives (sections 25.1 to 25.3)
Financial rigour The contribution bridge and the six-option comparison, both traced to model tables T5 and T15
Feasibility The 175-rider, zero-debt staffing and financing path, carried forward from research sections 22 and 23

Therefore, the case's own question, whether SwiftKart should electrify its existing fleet, pursue the growth opportunity, or combine both C O09, has one answer across all three lenses the judging criteria ask for C I08: do both, lease every bike, and spend the crore on what a lease cannot buy. The 88% growth in deliveries and the 56% cut in emissions a delivery are not a trade-off against each other, and the 4.9 times rise in contribution is not bought with debt or with a weaker service commitment; all three move together because the plan electrifies ahead of the contract rather than in response to it, keeps every vehicle leased rather than owned so the ₹1 crore funds the capabilities, working capital, charging, lease deposits, reporting, riders, a lease cannot buy, and never needs the one thing, bank debt, that every buy-based alternative requires in the bear case. If the contract is never awarded, the same sequencing still delivers an NPV of ₹3.34 crore and a fully electrified fleet two years ahead of Delhi's own regulatory clock; if it is awarded, the plan is already built to run it at the service level, emissions intensity and reporting standard the client's own contract requires. That is the business case this document makes, and it is the one the twelve-risk register, the four-gate roadmap, the two-lessor operating model and the fourteen-KPI monthly report in this part are built to keep honest as the plan is executed, not merely as it is pitched.

Exhibit for the deck: S4 The ₹1 Crore Decision, the moneyshot card (₹42 lakh to ₹2.06 crore, 4.9 times, three mini KPIs); S5 Recommendation and Roadmap, the KPI table (today, month 12, month 24).

What this section establishes, and what it does not

  • People, planet and profit are shown as one plan read through three lenses: 175 trained riders by month 8 T8, emissions intensity down 56% while deliveries rise 88% and absolute emissions fall 17% T14, and contribution up 4.9 times with zero debt in every scenario T5, T10, T15.
  • The scorecard (section 13, T6) independently confirms the same conclusion from a weighted multi-criteria method, scoring the recommended plan 5.00 out of 5, the maximum and the highest of six options.
  • The bull-case Scope 2 opportunity (green power under Delhi's Green Energy Open Access regulations, RG51) is flagged as an honest upside not counted in the headline emissions figure, consistent with this document's scenario discipline elsewhere.
  • This section closes the five-section arc of research sections 21 to 25 (risk, roadmap, operating model, KPIs, impact) by returning to the recommendation itself (research section 2), not by introducing a new analysis.
  • This section does not quantify the people lens in rupee terms, since the case brief provides no wage-welfare cost-benefit framework to apply; the people impact is reported through training coverage and onboarding structure, not a monetised figure, consistent with golden rule 4 against fabricating data that was not found.
  • This section does not revisit the deck's own slide-level moneyshot framing in detail, which research section 26 (writer G) carries forward into the Figma build specification.

26. The deck: four slides and an annexure, and where every number on them comes from

Answer. The submission is seven Figma Slides artefacts: a cover, the four counted slides the brief requires at S02 to S05 (The Situation, Strategic Alternatives, The ₹1 Crore Decision, Recommendation and Roadmap), an annexure slide that does not count against the four-slide cap per N02, and a thank-you slide. Every number on every slide traces to one of three places: a case fact tagged [C <ID>], an assumption tagged [A<NN>], or a model output tagged [M]/[T<N>], and this section builds the full trace for the headline figures on each slide. The deck's one moneyshot sits on S4: contribution rising from ₹42.2 L to ₹2.06 Cr a year by month 24, a 4.9 times increase, with ₹0 debt drawn [T5] [T15].

26.1 The seven-slide shape, and why it is seven, not four or eleven

S01's own submission requirements cap the counted deck at four slides (S01: "maximum 4-slide presentation, excluding the Title Slide and Annexure") [C S01], naming the four slides as The Situation, Strategic Alternatives, The ₹1 Crore Decision, and Recommendation & Roadmap [C S02] [C S03] [C S04] [C S05]. The annexure is explicitly outside that cap and may hold "detailed calculations, financial models, assumptions, sensitivity analysis, supporting research, sources" [C N01] [C N02]. The built deck therefore has seven Figma slides in total: a cover (not counted, conventional practice for a title page), the four counted slides in the brief's own order, one annexure slide (not four or five separate appendix pages, to keep the file to a single additional artefact rather than sprawl), and a thank-you slide (not counted, a closing courtesy). This matches the archetype plan the skill's T4 touchpoint confirmed at build time: cover as a hub-and-spoke mind map, S2 as a two-chart dense action-title slide, S3 as a MECE option filter plus a sensitivity heat map, S4 as the moneyshot plus three uses of capital, S5 as the implementation plan with gates and a risk matrix, S6 as the appendix (calculations, assumptions, tornado, scenarios, emissions, sources), and S7 as the conclusion synthesis ending on "THEREFORE".

26.2 Slide-by-slide blueprint

S1, Cover. Top band: a chip reading "IEEE DTU · DREAM FORGE 3.0 · ROUND 2", three logo slots for IEEE DTU, Dream Forge, and DTU, and the team chip. Title "THE ₹1 CRORE / CROSSROADS" with the subtitle "SwiftKart's next move: electrify, grow, or both, on ₹1 crore". A layered verdict card: "OUR ANSWER: DO BOTH, LEASE EVERY BIKE, AND SPEND THE CRORE ON WHAT A LEASE CANNOT BUY" followed by the cover line (electrify first, contribution to ₹2.06 Cr by month 24, no debt, ₹5.8 L of the crore in reserve). A team table (Harsh Kawatra, Team Leader, DTU; Dayita Arora, Member, Ramjas College, University of Delhi). On the right, a mind-map panel titled "WHO SHAPES THE CROSSROADS" with a seed line comparing the leased all-in cost (₹3,500) against the bought all-in cost (₹5,684), a central hub "SWIFTKART / 100 bikes", four spoke nodes, a dashed bus to five EV-maker crests, and fine print. The full node and logo-slot inventory is in 26.5.

S2, The Situation (deck slide 1 of 4). Headline: petrol takes 34% of every rupee SwiftKart earns and leaves ₹3,520 a bike a month; the ₹2.8 Cr contract assumes 100% use, not 85%. Three rails, bottom to top: TODAY, PRESSURE, THE CHALLENGE. Band 1 (today): four KPI tiles (100 bikes, ₹3.18 Cr revenue a year, ₹42.2 L contribution a year, 13.3% margin), a one-bike-month waterfall in ₹ thousand, and a five-row unit-economics table (Petrol, EV bought running-cost-only, EV bought all-in, EV leased, EV leased at contract's 100% use). Band 2 (pressure): a Delhi petrol line chart across five dated years, a three-row client-commitments panel with logos (Flipkart, Amazon, Blinkit), and a policy timeline of four dated milestones with a PM E-DRIVE footnote. Band 3 (the challenge): four numbered badges under "THE CONTRACT, READ CLOSELY" and a dark challenge card naming the ₹2.04 Cr twice-the-crore arithmetic, with three chips (FIX THE MARGIN, WIN THE CONTRACT, STAY LIQUID). Nine content forms in total.

S3, Strategic Alternatives (deck slide 2 of 4). Headline: leasing both fleets is worth ₹5.76 Cr over four years, ₹1.10 Cr more than buying both, which needs ₹110.0 L of debt. Two rails: SIX OPTIONS, TRADE-OFFS. Band 1: an eight-column options table (all six options, contract, capex, debt, NPV, run-rate, grams CO2, score), with row 4 (buy both) tinted red and row 6 (lease both) tinted teal, and a weighted-score horizontal-bar chart with the scorecard's own formula in a callout box. Band 2: a struck-through panel "THE OBVIOUS ANSWER: BUY BOTH" with three red badges (debt, EMI above lease, risk retained) and a "CONCLUSIVELY" callout naming the ₹5,153 switch point; a stacked-column chart of what a bike-month costs under petrol, bought, and leased configurations; and a seven-row by six-column diverging heat map of the case's own seven uncertainties against six options. Seven forms.

S4, The ₹1 Crore Decision (deck slide 3 of 4). Headline: the crore buys what a lease cannot: ₹94.1 L for working capital, charging, deposits, data and riders, and ₹5.8 L in reserve. Two rails: ALLOCATION, RETURNS. Band 1: a donut chart of the six uses of the ₹1 crore with a matching six-row table (use, ₹ lakh, share, when), and a three-line cash chart over nine points comparing the recommended plan, buying both, and staying petrol, with a loan annotation on the buy-both line. Band 2: the moneyshot card itself (₹42 L arrow ₹2.06 Cr, "4.9 the contribution of today, with ₹0 of debt and cash never below ₹1.02 Cr", three mini-KPIs for NPV gain, the margin over buying both, and the emissions cut), a six-step bridge waterfall turning ₹42.2 L into ₹206.0 L, and an eight-row "what has to be true" assumptions table. Six forms.

S5, Recommendation and Roadmap (deck slide 4 of 4). Headline: lease both fleets and electrify first, 175 EVs and no petrol by month 12, ₹2.06 Cr a year by month 24, and no debt. Three rails: THE ANSWER, ROADMAP, RISK AND KPIs. Band 1: a dark answer card with three bulleted reasons (value, liquidity, resilience) and a stacked-column chart of the fleet composition by quarter (petrol, EV existing, EV contract). Band 2: an eight-quarter Gantt with six workstreams and four gate diamonds (G1 to G4), plus a four-row "GO ONLY IF" gate-test table. Band 3: a 3x3 probability-by-impact risk grid, a five-badge risk/mitigation list (including the no-award branch's ₹1.88 Cr NPV gain over staying petrol and the renewal switch point), and a KPI table across today, month 12, and month 24. Seven forms.

S6, Annexure (not counted against the four-slide cap). A separate four-tag ribbon (A1 to A4), not the main deck's ribbon. A1: a quarterly calculations table (eight quarters: revenue, contribution, cash) plus two formula callouts (the bought-EV monthly arithmetic; the EMI arithmetic). A2: an eight-row bear/base/bull assumptions table. A3: a nine-input tornado chart, a four-row scenario table (NPV, run-rate, lowest cash, debt across bear, base, bull for the recommended plan), and a line naming the three switch points. A4: a three-row emissions table (today against month 24), a method callout (the kg-CO2 arithmetic for a petrol bike against an EV), and a twelve-line bibliography. Eight forms.

S7, Thank you. "THANK YOU" title, a dark "THEREFORE" synthesis card restating the full recommendation in one sentence, the team table repeated, three link slots (research document, financial model, Figma deck), and a closing line naming the model hash.

The cover's mind-map panel is a hub-and-spoke diagram with one hub, four spoke nodes, a dashed bus, and five EV- maker crests, matching the archetype the skill's generate-mode slide templates call a hub-and-spoke diagram for a cover that must orient the judge to every actor in the case before a single number appears.

Hub: "SWIFTKART / 100 bikes" [C D01], a filled circle at the panel's visual centre, connected to all four spoke nodes by diagonal wires.

A dashed horizontal bus runs below the four nodes to five EV-maker crest slots: Ather, TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto, Hero Vida, Kinetic Green, captioned "Electric two-wheeler makers selling in India", with fine print stating the logos mark companies referenced in the analysis and that no partnership is implied.
