What this section establishes, and what it does not

  • It establishes the exact slide-by-slide content of all seven Figma artefacts, with panel-level detail for every band, chart, table, and callout, matching the build files (deck/slides/s01.js through s07.js) and the research constants in deck/make_values.py.
  • It establishes a full derivation trail for the headline numbers on S2 through S5, so a judge who asks "where does ₹2.06 Cr come from" can be answered by naming a research section, a tag, and a model table in one breath.
  • It establishes the cover's complete mind-map and logo-slot inventory, including the count (seventeen slots) and the honest note that not every slot is guaranteed a secured brand asset at submission time.
  • It does not re-derive any number already derived in sections 2 through 25; it only traces each deck number back to where that derivation already lives.
  • It does not cover the annexure's A1 to A4 panels at the same line-by-line depth as S2 to S5, since the annexure itself restates model tables T7 through T16 directly and is its own citation.
  • It does not assess whether the deck is visually well executed; that is a Figma-build and critique-mode question (D6 in the build plan), not a research-document question.

27. Forty questions the judges are likely to ask, and our answers

This bank collects forty questions a demanding panel is likely to put to this submission, drawn from the case's own disclaimers (T05, T07, I07), the weakest links in the research lanes own gaps, and the places where the model's assumptions carry real judgement rather than verified fact. The ten hardest questions come first; the remaining thirty are grouped loosely by topic rather than ranked further.

Q1. "Your whole recommendation rests on a ₹3,500 all-in lease. No lane found a single verified, dated, Delhi-NCR, all-inclusive B2B quote at that price. What if real lessors quote ₹5,000 or more?" The ₹3,500 figure is the case own stated fact C D12, not our invention, and we say plainly that no lane verified an all-inclusive quote matching its exact scope RB37RB42. The bear case already assumes ₹5,000 A12, and at that rate leasing both still beats buying both on NPV (₹4.76 Cr against a lower buy-both bear of ₹1.35 Cr) T11. The fleet-level switch point is ₹5,153 a month T13; leasing only loses if a lessor refuses to hold a rate at or below that for 36 months, a kill criterion we checked and did not trigger M.

Q2. "The contract is the client decision, not yours. What does your recommendation actually buy if SwiftKart never wins it?" We size this explicitly as the no-award branch: lease the existing 100 bikes regardless, worth ₹3.34 Cr over 48 months, ₹1.88 Cr above staying petrol T5. The plan capital schedule electrifies the existing fleet in months 2, 4 and 12 independent of contract timing, so nothing is wasted if the award never lands C O06. The contract is roughly half the recommendation total value (₹5.76 Cr against ₹3.34 Cr without it), and we say so rather than implying the whole number depends on winning it T5.

Q3. "Your emissions numbers rest on a 42 km per litre fuel economy and a 0.036 kWh per km EV energy figure that no lane found specific to a loaded, stop-start delivery duty cycle. Why should we trust the 56 percent cut?" Both figures are conservative, not optimistic, against every comparison point found: real-world petrol commuter economy ranges 47 to 65 km per litre, an assumption check RD01, and maker-derived EV energy use for similar scooters clusters 16.5 to 30 Wh per km, also an assumption check RD15, both outside and more favourable to EVs than our bases. If anything, the true cut is larger than 56 percent, not smaller T14. The two factors that set the rupee-to-gram conversion, A21 and A24, were independently confirmed against the primary IPCC and CEA documents RG01RG40.

Q4. "A bought EV costs ₹3,000 a month to run once it is paid off, cheaper than the ₹3,500 lease. Why lease at all instead of buying and waiting out the capital cost?" We say this plainly rather than hide it: the recommended plan's month-24 run-rate (₹2.06 Cr) sits below buying both's run-rate (₹2.21 Cr) T5. Owning is cheaper to run once paid for; leasing wins on value over 48 months (₹5.76 Cr against ₹4.66 Cr), on liquidity (no debt against ₹110.0 L), and on resilience, not on monthly margin T5. In the bear case the run-rate gap widens (₹67.6 L against ₹1.156 Cr) and leasing still wins on NPV because buying then needs ₹140.0 L of debt T10.

Q5. "The case says a subsidy of ₹10,000 per EV may be available, not that it is guaranteed. What happens to your buy-side comparisons if it never arrives?" We read may be available literally in section 4.7 rather than treating it as certain C X06. Removing the subsidy raises a bought EV's monthly-equivalent cost further above the lease (the capital component alone rises by about ₹60 a month once the ₹10,000 credit is removed from the annuity), an assumption-level check T3. This widens, not narrows, leasing's advantage. The subsidy question cuts toward, not against, the recommendation; the kill criterion tied to a far larger subsidy (₹90,000 or more) was checked and not triggered, with the real ceiling closer to ₹35,000 to ₹40,000 RE33.

Q6. "You moved the contract receivable-days assumption from 45 to 57 using Delhivery and Blue Dart as comparables. What if SwiftKart's own client pays even slower, say 75 days?" We modelled exactly that in the sensitivity table: at 75 days the recommended plan's NPV falls only to ₹5.72 Cr from ₹5.76 Cr, the smallest swing of the nine inputs tested T11. Working capital is the largest single use of the crore at ₹44.5 L precisely because we assumed realistic payment terms rather than the earlier, friendlier 45-day planning estimate T9. The reserve (₹5.8 L) is thinner than an earlier draft's ₹15.2 L as a direct result, and we disclose that honestly rather than keep the more comfortable number, a plain assumption note T9.

Q7. "Leasing moves battery and resale risk onto the lessor, but the lessor must price that risk into the ₹3,500 rate somewhere. Are you not just paying for that risk indirectly either way?" Yes, and we do not claim otherwise: a lease rate embeds the lessor's own risk premium, which is exactly why the rate matters so much and why we tested it against a ₹5,153 fleet-level switch point rather than assume ₹3,500 is permanent T13. The difference is who bears the risk if the outcome is worse than priced: a lessor spreads battery and resale risk across many fleets, while SwiftKart alone would bear all of an unlucky battery-life or resale outcome under ownership. Shifting variance to a party better placed to pool it is a standard risk-transfer argument, an assumption we name as such A26, not a claim that the risk disappears.

Q8. "The case says there is no single predetermined correct answer. Why should we accept leasing both as the answer rather than one defensible option among several?" We do not claim it is the only defensible path; we claim it scores highest on the scorecard built from the case's own evaluation axes (value, liquidity, resilience, emissions, growth) at 5.00 out of 5, against buying both's 3.65 T6, and it is the only one of six options with zero debt and the highest NPV simultaneously T5. Buying both is a genuinely strong second option, named fairly as the obvious answer with its real strengths (the highest run-rate contribution, the second-highest NPV) stated before its weaknesses T5. The case's own disclaimer is honoured by showing our reasoning in full, not by refusing to recommend.

Q9. "CEA's grid emission factor may have fallen since the version you used (0.727). If the true current figure is closer to 0.675, does that not undermine your 56 percent cut?" A lower grid factor would strengthen, not undermine, the emissions case: a cleaner grid makes the EV side of the comparison cleaner too, which widens the gap in the recommendation's favour, an assumption-level point RG40. We used v20.0 (December 2024) because it is the newest version this environment could download and read directly from the primary PDF; v21.0 and v22.0 exist per secondary reports but sit behind a login wall we could not clear RG43. We disclose this honestly in section 12.2 rather than quietly use an unverified newer number.

Q10. "Alt Mobility reportedly leases at around ₹2,800 a month, well below your ₹3,500 case figure. If the real market is cheaper, is your own model too conservative, and should the recommendation be even stronger than stated?" Quite possibly, and we say so: the ₹2,800 figure is a verified lane finding RB19, but it comes bundled on a 3 to 5 year term with a scope that is reasonably, not exactly, comparable to the case's all-in framing, so we did not substitute it for the case's own ₹3,500 fact C D12. We kept the case's own number as the base case per the brief's instruction to work from the data provided, and flagged the possible further upside as an honest gap rather than a quiet improvement to our own numbers, an assumption-level note RB19.

Q11. "Why discount at 11 percent rather than a higher venture-style hurdle rate given this is a small operator?" The 11 percent rate is the case's own stated bank loan rate C X08, used as the cost-of-capital proxy per standard practice when a case does not supply a separate discount rate. The bear scenario raises it to 15 percent to capture an equity-risk premium A14, and the recommended plan's NPV only falls to ₹6.02 Cr at that sensitivity band's low end, the sixth-largest of nine tested swings T11, so the recommendation is not rate-sensitive enough to overturn the ranking.

Q12. "Why not finance the lease itself with debt and keep more cash on hand even earlier?" The recommended plan already draws zero debt in every scenario, including bear T10, so adding debt to fund a lease would only add interest cost without funding anything the ₹1 crore cannot already cover; the sources- and-uses reconciliation in section 17.4 shows the crore plus petrol-sale proceeds fully fund the plan without borrowing T9.

Q13. "Under Ind AS 116 a lease still creates a liability on the balance sheet. Does calling this no debt not overstate the liquidity benefit?" We do not claim the lease is invisible on the books; section 20.4 states plainly that Ind AS 116 recognises a lease liability regardless, an assumption-framed point RB82. No debt in this document means no bank borrowing and no interest cost drawn against the loan facility, which is the distinction that actually matters for cash floor and covenant risk; the 36-month SwiftKart lease sits close to, though not clearly over, the 75 percent economic-life threshold that would force finance-lease treatment under AS 19, a genuine judgement call we name rather than resolve RB83.

Q14. "Delhi's new-registration electric-only rule starts April 2028, outside your 24-month window. Why does the policy clock matter to a 24-month plan at all?" Because a separate, earlier rule bites first: Delhi EV Policy 2026 and CAQM Direction 94 bar NCR fleet aggregators from inducting any new petrol vehicle, including two-wheelers, after 31 December 2026, well inside the 24-month horizon RE37RE38. The recommended plan already has zero petrol bikes by month 12 T8, so it clears that date with a year to spare regardless of the later 2028 rule.

Q15. "Battery degradation evidence conflicts by up to six times across sources. How confident can you really be in 10 spares and a 95 percent availability target?" Not fully confident, and we say so in section 11.2: three sources disagree sharply on cycle life, and we flagged that conflict rather than pick the most convenient one, a conflict on record as C-D2. The 10-spares sizing is built to a 95 percent availability assumption A15, with a stated bear case of 90 percent; if real degradation sits at the pessimistic end of the range, the fix is more spares or shorter swap cycles, an operating response, not a reason to abandon leasing, since the lessor, not SwiftKart, carries the asset-level battery-replacement risk.

Q16. "Your dispatch-pooling benefit, an 11-point utilisation gain, comes from a vendor's own illustrative model, not a measured result. Is that not too thin a foundation to rely on?" Yes, and section 23.4's own title names it an association, not proof, stated honestly as such, an assumption we flag plainly [RF]. The recommended plan's core numbers, NPV, cash, debt, do not depend on pooling succeeding; pooling is an upside lever inside the operating model, not a load-bearing assumption in the financial case.

Q17. "Rider pay rise is modelled at 0.0 percent in the base case even though Delhi's verified minimum wage (₹18,456 a month) sits well above the case's stated ₹14,000 rider pay. Is your base case not unrealistic?" We hold rider pay flat in base deliberately because the case gives ₹14,000 as a fact to work from C D05, and we model the minimum-wage pressure explicitly in the bull case at plus 10 percent from month 13 A16, cross-referenced to the verified ₹18,456 figure RE75. The tornado shows a rider-pay rise costs the recommended plan ₹1.02 Cr of NPV swing, the fifth-largest of nine inputs, material but not decisive T11.

Q18. "Why does the plan delay 10 of the 100 existing bikes to month 12 instead of converting all 100 at once?" The last 10 are a deliberate fallback wave, held as a buffer against contract-timing uncertainty: converting slower than the first two waves, 50 in month 2 and 40 in month 4, keeps capital and rider-training capacity free while the contract ramps, rather than converting the full fleet before contract volume and its own 75-EV schedule is confirmed, a scheduling assumption tied to C O06.

Q19. "Your scorecard weights, 0.35 value, 0.20 liquidity, 0.20 resilience, 0.15 emissions, 0.10 growth, look chosen to favour leasing. How do we know the weights are not reverse-engineered from the answer?" The weights were fixed before scoring, stated as a rule in section 13.4, and every band, 1 to 5, for every criterion was defined in advance of computing a single option's score T6. The recommendation also wins on raw NPV alone, ₹5.76 Cr, the highest of six, without any scoring weights applied at all T5, so the ranking does not depend on the weighting scheme to hold.

Q20. "The contract requires monthly emissions reporting, but your own challenge card on S2 says SwiftKart does not currently collect that data. Is that not a feasibility gap in your own plan?" Yes, which is exactly why ₹13.0 L of the crore is allocated to building a reporting and dispatch platform before the contract ramps, not after T9. The plan sequences electrification and reporting-system build in months 2 to 8, ahead of the contract's own ramp in months 4 to 10, specifically so the capability exists before the client needs the first monthly report C O06.

Q21. "You assume 100 percent plateau utilisation for the contract's ₹2.8 crore figure, but SwiftKart's own fleet only runs at 85 percent today. Is that not inconsistent?" It is the case's own figure, not an assumption we introduced: O07 states the contract generates approximately ₹2.8 crore in annual revenue at full capacity C O07, which the arithmetic, 75 times 30 times 26 times ₹40 times 12, only reconciles at 100 percent utilisation M. We name this inconsistency explicitly in section 4.1 rather than silently assume the contract runs at SwiftKart's own 85 percent, and our bear case for contract volume, A09 and A11, models something closer to that lower, more cautious utilisation.

Q22. "What if EV acquisition costs fall faster than modelled, case uncertainty U02? Does that not eventually favour buying over leasing?" Possibly, over a long enough horizon, which is exactly why the plan keeps a real option rather than commit irreversibly: at month 36's lease renewal, SwiftKart buys instead if the lease reprices above ₹5,153 a month, and falling EV prices would only make that buy option cheaper if exercised T13. The sensitivity table shows a 15 percent EV price fall moves the recommended plan's NPV down by only ₹4.2 lakh at most, the smallest- magnitude shock tested against the recommendation, since leasing already avoids the capital exposure that a price fall would otherwise help, a case-uncertainty result T12.

Q23. "Why build a reporting and dispatch platform, ₹13.0 L to ₹17.0 L, rather than buy an off-the-shelf telematics package, which no lane found priced for this exact combined scope?" Because no lane found a vendor selling a combined telematics-plus-GHG-Protocol-method-plus-pooled-dispatch build at any disclosed price; every product found, LocoNav, Watsoo, TechnoPurple, is GPS tracking alone, a materially narrower scope, an honest gap we flag rather than paper over [RF]. The ₹13.0 L figure is an unmatched modelling estimate, disclosed as such, not a vendor quote we are claiming to have sourced.

Q24. "Your tornado chart puts price per delivery as the single largest swing factor, ₹3.62 Cr. If SwiftKart's real per-delivery rate turns out lower than ₹40, does the whole recommendation not collapse?" At the tested low end, ₹36 a delivery, the recommended plan's NPV is still ₹3.95 Cr, the lowest point in the entire tornado but still comfortably above staying petrol's base case of ₹1.45 Cr T11. Price per delivery is the case's own stated fact, ₹40, D02, and our sensitivity test only varies it to show the plan's margin of safety, not because we doubt the case figure.

Q25. "GST treatment differs between buying an EV, 5 percent, and leasing one for business use, 18 percent per the Odisha AAAR ruling. Does the tax gap not erode leasing's cost advantage?" The 13-point GST gap is real and disclosed in section 10.5, but it applies to a service charge on a monthly rate that is already less than half the all-in bought cost, ₹3,500 against ₹5,684; even adding an 18 percent load to the lease rate, about ₹630 a month, would leave leasing below the bought all-in cost, an assumption-level check RB118, so the tax differential does not flip the comparison.

Q26. "Shadowfax's own client concentration runs near 60 to 75 percent. If SwiftKart's contract client leaves after a year, as Ecom Express lost Meesho, does your contract-is-half-the-value framing not understate the concentration risk?" We cite that precedent explicitly in section 7.4 as the honest basis for treating the contract as a re-tenderable relationship, not a guaranteed multi-year annuity, a precedent-based assumption [RH]. That is precisely why the no-award branch is modelled and sized, ₹3.34 Cr, rather than assumed away: if the client leaves after the contract window, the existing-fleet leasing plan alone still beats staying petrol by ₹1.88 Cr T5.

Q27. "Your risk register lists twelve risks. Why these twelve and not, say, twenty, given how many uncertainties the case itself names, U01 to U07?" Every one of the case's own seven uncertainties maps directly onto at least one of the twelve risks, section 21.1's own cross-reference table, and the twelve were built to MECE-cover financing, operations, and policy/reporting rather than to hit a round number; three of the twelve carry little or no cost to this specific plan and are named as such rather than padded for volume C U01 through C U07.

Q28. "A pre-mortem is a useful exercise, but how do we know your three failure stories in section 21.6 are not just restatements of risks you already planned around?" They are deliberately built from the model's own numbers rather than left as unquantified narrative: each story is checked against a specific model output, for example what happens to cash if the contract slips past month 8, rather than invented freely, which is the discipline that keeps a pre-mortem from becoming generic worry.

Q29. "Heatwave and monsoon disruption to rider fulfilment is well documented in Delhi, but no source quantifies a fulfilment-rate drop for a two-wheeler fleet. How did you handle that gap?" We logged it as the section's central, unresolved gap rather than invent a number, an honest assumption-level note [RF]. The 95 percent fulfilment target already carries a 5-point buffer against exactly this kind of disruption; the spares pool, 10 vehicles, and the two-lessor split both exist partly to absorb exactly this unquantified risk operationally rather than model it financially.

Q30. "Why size the cash floor, A25, at ₹10 lakh rather than a larger buffer given the thinner reserve you disclosed?" ₹10 lakh is set to roughly one month of rider pay for the contract fleet, a liquidity rule of thumb, an assumption we name as such A25. Even in the bear scenario the plan's lowest cash point, ₹63.0 L, sits well above that floor T10, so the ₹10 lakh threshold, though thinner than first drafted, is never actually breached across any scenario tested.

Q31. "If leasing both fleets is this clearly superior, why would any fleet operator in Delhi-NCR still choose to buy EVs outright?" Buying wins when an operator already has cheap capital, plans to run the asset well past 48 months, or values owning the asset for resale optionality; our own numbers show buying both has the second-highest NPV and the highest run-rate contribution of the six options T5, so it is a reasonable choice under a different capital structure or risk appetite, not an irrational one.

Q32. "Your EMI figure of ₹3,601 assumes a specific loan structure. What if SwiftKart can negotiate a cheaper rate than the case's 11 percent?" The real market for this borrower type runs 8.50 percent to 24 percent across named banks and NBFCs RB76RB77, so 11 percent sits at the cheap end already; even at the lowest verified bank rate the EMI would still exceed ₹3,500, since the principal, ₹1,10,000 net of subsidy, is the larger driver of the EMI than the rate itself.

Q33. "The contract's 95 percent fulfilment requirement is a service-level clause. What happens to the economics if SwiftKart misses it and faces a penalty?" No lane found a quantified, India-specific contractual penalty clause for missed fulfilment in this market, an honest assumption-level gap [RC], so no penalty cost sits in the model; this is disclosed as a gap rather than assumed at zero by omission, and operationally the plan's spares and two-lessor redundancy are built specifically to keep fulfilment at or above 95 percent rather than rely on a penalty-free assumption.

Q34. "Why choose two lessors rather than one, if that adds coordination overhead?" Splitting the fleet across two lessors is a direct hedge against the single largest operational risk named in the register, a lessor failing to deliver vehicles or swap batteries on schedule; the coordination cost is modelled inside the existing contract operations overhead line, ₹1.5 lakh a month, A07, rather than treated as free.

Q35. "You cite the ICCT's 2021 working paper for TCO comparisons. That paper is international and several years old. Is it still representative of 2026 Indian delivery economics?" We treat it as the best available independently-reviewed TCO study for this exact vehicle class, not as a perfectly current figure, and cross-check its directional finding, petrol most expensive, point charging cheapest, against our own case-specific arithmetic rather than importing its absolute rupee figures wholesale, an assumption-level cross-check RD276. Where our own model's case-based numbers differ from the paper's, we use the case's own numbers, as the task requires.

Q36. "Your rider onboarding cost, ₹5,000, A03, was not matched to any single verified source. Is that number reliable?" No single source verifies it exactly, and we say so in the build log: the nearest verified fragments, Shadowfax's ₹1,000 rider-paid deduction, PMJJBY and PMSBY premiums of roughly ₹350 to ₹420 a year, wholesale helmet prices of ₹710 to ₹1,000, are consistent with a ₹4,000 to ₹7,000 range but do not pin ₹5,000 to one named source, an assumption we disclose as such [RF]. It remains a disclosed modelling estimate within that plausible band.

Q37. "Your emissions-reporting plan assumes a GHG Protocol and ISO 14083 method, but the case only asks for monthly reporting of emissions-related metrics. Are you over-engineering the compliance burden?" The standards' own minimum cadence is annual, so the case's monthly requirement already exceeds, not merely implements, ISO 14083 and the GLEC Framework, an assumption-level reading of the standard RG37. Building to the recognised standard from the outset avoids a costly later re-build once the client very plausibly asks for assured, standards-aligned disclosure, which several named clients already require of their own suppliers under BRSR Core.

Q38. "Why does the plan assume the contract starts at month 3 to 5 rather than immediately?" Month 3, base case, with a bear case of month 5 and a bull case of month 2, reflects the time a large e-commerce client typically takes for negotiation, audit, and onboarding of a new logistics partner, an assumption so flagged A08. The tornado shows award timing is the second-smallest swing of the nine inputs tested, ₹0.29 Cr, so the exact month does not materially change the recommendation T11.

Q39. "If staying petrol only loses ₹4.31 crore of NPV relative to your plan, and petrol is the status quo with zero execution risk, why not just recommend doing nothing for now and reassess next year?" Doing nothing carries its own quietly compounding risk: Delhi bars new petrol fleet inductions after 31 December 2026 RE37, and staying petrol leaves the ₹2.8 Cr contract opportunity entirely on the table, which is itself worth more than the whole existing-fleet electrification decision T5. Waiting and seeing is not risk-free; it is a different, worse bet, and the model quantifies exactly how much worse, ₹4.31 Cr, rather than leaving it as a vague caution.

Q40. "Teams were told there is no single predetermined correct answer and will be evaluated on creativity as well as rigour. Where is the creativity in this submission beyond a careful spreadsheet?" The creative move is the one the obvious reading of the case prompt misses: the case frames the decision as buy-versus-lease-versus-grow, but the governing insight, that a lease converts a ₹1,20,000 capital decision into a ₹3,500 operating decision and frees the crore for things a lease cannot buy, working capital, data systems, deposits, training, is not visible from the case's own fleet-alternatives table alone; it required reading the lease line, D12, against the full cost of ownership, D10, D13, D14, rather than against running cost alone T3, which is exactly the comparison most buy-side arguments skip.

27.3 How to use this bank in the room

Three patterns recur across the forty answers above, and a presenter should recognise them rather than treat each answer as a one-off script. The first pattern is concede, then redirect: on every question that names a genuine weakness, Q1, Q5, Q6, Q7, Q9, Q13, Q15, Q16, Q23, Q29, Q33 and Q36 all concede the weakness in the first sentence before showing why it does not change the recommendation, because a panel that hears a flat denial of an obviously real gap trusts the rest of the answer less, not more. The second pattern is numbers over adjectives: every answer leads with a figure and its tag rather than a qualitative reassurance, since "the bear case still clears the threshold" persuades a judging panel far less than "₹5.72 Cr against a base of ₹5.76 Cr, the smallest swing of the nine inputs tested T11." The third pattern is the no-award branch as the all-purpose backstop: Q2, Q21, Q26 and Q39 all resolve, at bottom, to the same fact, that leasing the existing 100 bikes alone is worth ₹3.34 Cr regardless of what happens to the contract, and a presenter under pressure can return to that one number whenever a question tries to make the whole recommendation hinge on the contract being won.

Four of the forty questions deserve a specific presentation note beyond their written answer. Q8 and Q40, both about the case's own no-single-correct-answer disclaimer, should be answered by pointing at the scorecard table on S3 rather than relitigating the disclaimer in words, since the scorecard is the artefact that shows the comparison was run fairly rather than asserted. Q1 and Q9, both about a number that could move against the recommendation (the real lease rate, the grid factor), should be answered by naming the specific model table that already tests the adverse case (T11's sensitivity row, T10's bear scenario) rather than promising to "look into it," since the whole point of building the sensitivity analysis in advance is to have the adverse-case number ready rather than improvised.

One worked example makes the concede-then-redirect pattern concrete rather than asserted. Q1's defence rests on two already-modelled numbers, not a new calculation: the fleet-level switch point of ₹5,153 a month T13 and the bear-case lease rate of ₹5,000 a month A12, which sits ₹153 below that switch point. Shown as arithmetic: NPV of leasing both in the bear case is ₹4.76 Cr against ₹1.35 Cr for buying both in the bear case T10, a gap of ₹3.41 Cr that only closes if the real lease rate clears ₹5,153 a month, a rate 47% above the case's own ₹3,500 figure and 3% above even the bear-case rate already tested. The same discipline applies to Q19's scorecard formula: Score equals 0.35 Value plus 0.20 Liquidity plus 0.20 Resilience plus 0.15 Emissions plus 0.10 Growth T6, and option 6's total of 5.00 out of 5 is simply five fives multiplied by their own weights and summed: 0.35 times 5 is 1.75, 0.20 times 5 is 1.00, 0.20 times 5 is 1.00, 0.15 times 5 is 0.75, 0.10 times 5 is 0.50, and 1.75 plus 1.00 plus 1.00 plus 0.75 plus 0.50 equals 5.00 T6. A result built this way cannot be reverse-engineered from a single changed weight, since every band on every criterion, 1 to 5, was fixed before a single option was scored, and the formula itself sits in section 13.4 in full rather than only in this answer bank.

A final honest note on scope: this bank is deliberately adversarial by instruction, built to surface the sharpest objections a panel could raise rather than to flatter the submission. Several of the forty answers, Q6, Q15, Q23, Q29 and Q36 above all, concede that a specific input rests on a disclosed assumption or an unmatched modelling estimate rather than a verified figure. That is a feature of this document's own discipline, not a flaw to be talked around in the room: the research document distinguishes a case fact from an assumption from a model output from an outside source everywhere a number appears, precisely so that a question like these forty can be answered by naming which of the four categories the contested number falls into, rather than by restating the number more confidently than the evidence supports it.

28. Method, limits and the validation we would run next

Answer. Every number in this document falls into one of three categories, and the distinction matters because each carries a different kind of confidence: desk research is a fact someone else measured and published, drawn from a verified or corrected raw-data row and cited to its source; model output is an arithmetic result this document's own spreadsheet produced from case facts and assumptions, cited to a model table; and an assumption is a judgement this team made where the case or the research left a gap, cited to its assumption ID and stated as such at least once in the paragraph that uses it. None of the three categories is primary research conducted by this team on SwiftKart's actual riders, lessors, or clients, and this section says so plainly before listing what would need to happen, and roughly how long each step would take, to turn the recommendation from a desk-and-model case into a field-tested one.

28.1 What is desk research, what is model output, and what is assumption, with one example of each

A desk-research fact is a number this team found in a published, dated source and verified by cross-checking it against a second source where one existed, logged with its raw-fact ID and source ID. Example: the Delhi petrol price of ₹102.12 a litre, confirmed live as of 15 October 2026 by two independent sources RD11RD12, used in the model as A20. A model-output number is an arithmetic result this document's own spreadsheet computed from case facts and assumptions already fed into it, never typed in by hand a second time. Example: the recommended plan's NPV of ₹5.76 Cr over 48 months T5, which the model computes from the monthly cash flows in T7, each of which in turn traces to case facts (fleet size, revenue per delivery) and assumptions (contract award month, lease rate). An assumption is a number this team chose because neither the case nor the verified research supplied one, always disclosed as such in the paragraph that first uses it and carried in the assumptions register with a bear and bull range. Example: new rider onboarding cost of ₹5,000 A03, which section 27's Q36 already discloses rests on a consistent but not single-sourced range of ₹4,000 to ₹7,000, rather than one named vendor quote.

Category Example number Tag Where it is established
Desk research Delhi petrol price, ₹102.12 a litre, confirmed live 15 October 2026 by two independent sources RD11RD12 section 8.2
Model output Recommended plan NPV over 48 months, ₹5.76 Cr T5 section 18.6
Assumption New rider onboarding cost, ₹5,000 A03 section 23.2; Q36 of section 27

Table: one worked example of each of the three categories this section opened with, each tied to the tag and section that already establishes it, so a reader can see the distinction applied rather than only defined.

The practical test for a reader is this: if a number appears in T1 through T17 of model_tables.md with no [A] tag attached anywhere it is used, it is either a case fact restated unchanged (tag [C <ID>]) or a pure arithmetic derivation of case facts (tag [M] or a table tag such as [T2]); if it carries an [A] tag anywhere, it is a judgement call, and the assumptions register (T16) states its base, bear, and bull values and the basis for each. This document never blends the three categories inside one unlabelled sentence; every paragraph that cites a number also carries that number's tag, so the category is never left for the reader to infer.

These limits do not change the recommendation. Every one of them was already tested, where testable, against a bear case or a sensitivity band in sections 17 through 21, and the plan clears its own cash floor and keeps the highest NPV of six options even at the pessimistic end of every tested range T10T11. What the limits mean is narrower than "the answer might be wrong": they mean the margin of safety, while real, rests on model logic and published comparables rather than on a direct measurement of SwiftKart's own operation, and the validation plan below exists specifically to close that gap before, not after, capital is committed.

28.3 The validation plan: none of it has been run yet

None of the four steps below has been run. No lessor has been sent a request for proposal, no client service-level term has been reviewed with a named client, no rider has been timed on a route, and no emissions-reporting pilot has been built or tested. Everything in this subsection is a plan for what this team would do next, not a report of work already completed, and it is presented that way deliberately, since claiming otherwise would be exactly the kind of fabricated primary research this document's own discipline (section 0, the tag legend) exists to prevent.

Step What it would test Who runs it Roughly how long What a pass looks like

Table: four validation steps, none run yet, each tied to the specific number or capability in this document it would confirm or correct, with a rough duration built from general procurement, pilot, and reporting-cycle practice rather than from any measured timeline specific to this case.

These four steps are sequenced, not simultaneous, by design. The lessor RFP and the client SLA review should start first and run in parallel, since both feed directly into contract negotiation and the lease-deposit line of the ₹1 crore allocation (₹12.9 lakh, T9); the rider time-and-motion pilot should start once the first wave of 50 existing-fleet EVs is on the road in month 2 C O06, since it needs real vehicles to observe rather than a simulated route; and the emissions-reporting pilot should start once that same first wave has produced at least one full month of operating data, so the report it produces reflects real telematics output rather than a test file. Run this way, all four steps can complete inside the plan's own first two quarters, before the contract's own plateau volume arrives in month 8 to 10 A10, which is also before gate G2 (month 8) in the roadmap of section 22, so a lessor-RFP or SLA-review finding that moved a number materially would still arrive in time to adjust the plan at a gate rather than after capital already committed past it.

28.4 What a failed validation step would change, and what it would not

A validation step is only useful if its honest failure mode is stated in advance, not improvised afterward. If the lessor RFP returns no quote at or below ₹5,153 a month, the fleet-level switch point itself is the trigger already built into the plan: lease at the best rate found if it still beats buying on NPV, or shift the contract fleet to option 4 (lease for the contract, keep the existing fleet petrol a while longer) if it does not, rather than holding the whole recommendation hostage to one number. If the client SLA review finds a fulfilment-penalty clause large enough to matter, that cost enters the model as a new line item in the next model revision, a change this document would flag explicitly rather than absorb silently. If the rider time-and-motion pilot measures utilisation below 80%, the recommendation does not automatically fail, since the sensitivity table already shows the NPV at 80% utilisation (₹5.16 Cr, T11) comfortably above every other option's base case; only a result materially below 80% would require rework. If the emissions-reporting pilot finds the planned ₹13.0 lakh platform under-built for the client's actual format, the fix is a larger reporting-and-dispatch budget line, drawn from the ₹5.8 lakh reserve T9 first, not a reason to abandon monthly reporting altogether, since the contract itself requires it C O05.

Validation step If it fails What changes What does not change
Lessor RFP No quote clears ₹5,153 a month at the fleet-level switch point T13 The contract fleet shifts toward option 4 (lease for the contract, keep the existing fleet petrol longer) if leasing no longer beats buying on NPV at the real rate found The existing-fleet electrification already under way in months 2 to 4 C O06, which does not depend on the contract fleet's lease rate
Client SLA term review A fulfilment-penalty clause or a reporting format the planned platform cannot produce is found The penalty cost or a larger reporting-platform budget enters the next model revision as a new, flagged line item The requirement to report monthly, which the contract already states C O05 and which this plan already builds toward regardless of the review's outcome

Table: the failure mode of each validation step, what it would change in the plan, and what it would leave unchanged, stated in advance so a judge can see this team has thought through the downside of testing, not only the upside.

None of the four steps, even in its failure mode, overturns the core comparison this document rests on: leasing both fleets has the highest NPV of six options under every tested scenario, including bear T5T10, and the no-award branch alone is still worth ₹1.88 Cr more than staying petrol T5. Validation exists to firm up the confidence behind that comparison and to catch a cost this desk exercise could not see, not to re-open a question the sensitivity analysis in sections 17 through 21 has already stress-tested.

What this section establishes, and what it does not

  • It establishes a clear three-way split, desk research, model output, assumption, with one worked example of each, and the practical tag-based test a reader can apply to any number in this document to tell which category it falls into.
  • It establishes seven honest limits to what this document can claim, each already acknowledged somewhere earlier in the document and collected here in one place, and states plainly that none of them changes the recommendation as tested against the bear case and the sensitivity table.
  • It establishes a four-step validation plan, a lessor RFP, a client SLA term review, a rider time-and-motion study on a pilot of ten EVs, and an emissions-reporting pilot, each with what it would test, who would run it, and a rough duration, and states at the outset that none of the four has been run.
  • It establishes a sequencing and a failure-mode discussion for the validation plan, so a judge can see not only what would be tested but what a bad result from each test would and would not change about the recommendation.
  • It does not claim any of the four validation steps has started or produced a result; every figure it cites in support of a failure-mode discussion is a model output or a case fact already derived elsewhere in this document, never a fabricated field finding.
  • It does not reopen the model, the recommendation, or the ranking of the six options; it only states, honestly, what stands between a desk-and-model case and a field-tested one, and how this team would close that gap next.

29. Go-to-market: six large buyers, five with public EV targets, three aiming for 100% EV by 2030, and one anchor contract to land first

Answer. SwiftKart's go-to-market funnel runs from six named large Indian e-commerce and quick-commerce buyers, to five of them carrying a company-authored public EV commitment, to three stating a 2030 100% EV target specifically, to one anchor contract SwiftKart is pursuing today, 75 vehicles at ₹2.8 crore of annual revenue at full capacity [C O02] [C O07], with a second client by month 24 named only as a goal [M]. Every count in this funnel traces to a named, dated source: Flipkart, Amazon India, Zomato (through Eternal), Swiggy and BigBasket each carry a company-authored electrification commitment [RC02, RC12, RC19, RC25, RC40], Flipkart, Zomato and Swiggy each state a 2030, 100% target specifically [RC02, RC19, RC25], and Zepto is the sixth named buyer with no company-authored target, documented only through its fleet-provider partnerships with Zypp Electric and Yulu [RC33, RC34, RI01]. No conversion rate, win probability, or close rate appears anywhere in this section; the funnel counts named companies and dated commitments, not a sales pipeline with invented odds attached to each stage.

29.1 Stage one: six named buyers, each independently documented across two research lanes

Six companies anchor this funnel, each appearing independently in both lane R-C's client-commitment research (part-B section 6) and lane R-I's fleet-partner precedent research (this document's own new lane): Flipkart, Amazon India, Zomato (through its listed parent, Eternal), Swiggy, BigBasket and Zepto. Each of the six is a large enough buyer of last-mile delivery capacity that an EV-native fleet provider, Zypp Electric, Yulu, Mahindra Last Mile Mobility or Bounce, has built a named, dated commercial relationship with it: Zypp Electric alone names Zomato, Swiggy, BigBasket, Amazon, Flipkart, Zepto and Blinkit among more than 50 major clients it serves as of 26 April 2023 [RI15], which is independent, third-party confirmation that all six companies named in SwiftKart's own go-to-market funnel already buy third-party EV fleet capacity at scale, not a theoretical market SwiftKart would be the first operator to approach.

29.2 Stage two: five of six carry a company-authored public EV commitment

Of the six, five, Flipkart, Amazon India, Zomato (Eternal), Swiggy and BigBasket, carry a dated, company-authored electrification commitment, stated directly by the company or an exchange filing, not inferred from a partner's own marketing [RC02, RC12, RC19, RC25, RC40]. The sixth, Zepto, is the one documented exception: its own chief operating officer is quoted saying only that "a majority" of deliveries use "environment-friendly vehicles," with no percentage or deadline stated by Zepto itself [RC34], and the research document states this gap honestly rather than inferring a Zepto-authored target from the scale of its Yulu and Zypp Electric partnerships [RC33, RI01]. This stage-two count, five of six, is the one every subsequent stage of the funnel narrows from, and every number in it is a direct, named company statement, never averaged, blended, or estimated across the six.

29.3 Stage three: three of six name a 2030, 100% target specifically

Narrowing further, three of the five commitments above are not just dated and company-authored but specifically a 100% target by 2030: Flipkart's EV100 pledge is complete transition to electric vehicles by 2030 [RC07], Zomato's parent Eternal's own stated goal is a 100% EV delivery fleet by 2030 [RC19], and Swiggy's exchange filing states a target of transitioning to a 100% EV delivery fleet by 2030 [RC25]. 29.4 Stage four: one anchor contract, 75 vehicles, ₹2.8 crore at full capacity

The anchor contract is the case's own opportunity [C O01]: if secured, SwiftKart adds approximately 75 vehicles within 12 months [C O02], against requirements of minimum 95% delivery fulfilment [C O03], a significant low-emission vehicle share [C O04], monthly emissions-metric reporting [C O05], and the ability to scale within 12 months [C O06], generating approximately ₹2.8 crore in annual revenue at full capacity [C O07]. Shadowfax's own disclosed client concentration, about 74% of revenue from four named clients [RA35], is the comparable-operator norm this document reads SwiftKart's forthcoming single-contract dependence against: a concentration this large is the industry pattern at this scale of last-mile operator, not an anomaly specific to SwiftKart.

Revenue from top client group one contract, close to half of combined revenue about 74% from four named clients RA35
Scale of the comparable 100 bikes today, 175 vehicles after award 2,05,864 average quarterly delivery partners (Sep 2025) [C B01, T8, RA32]

Shadowfax operates three orders of magnitude larger than SwiftKart and still discloses concentration above 70% to 80%; this is read as confirmation that single-contract dependence at SwiftKart's own scale sits inside, not beyond, the range a comparable listed operator discloses as normal, not as proof that concentration carries no risk, a risk addressed directly in research section 21's register (R3, R5).

29.5 Land and expand as a staged plan, not a single leap

The recommended plan's own sequencing, electrify first, then add the contract fleet in three tranches across months 4, 6 and 8 [M], is itself a land-and-expand structure applied inside the single anchor contract before any second client is sought. "Land" is securing and fulfilling the one contract at the 95% floor [C O03]; "expand" within that same relationship means the contract's own phased vehicle additions (25 EVs in each of three tranches, 75 riders hired) rather than a single 75-vehicle commitment on day one [C O02], which lets SwiftKart demonstrate fulfilment and emissions-reporting capability on a smaller volume before the client's full expected revenue arrives. Land-and-expand toward a second client follows the same logic, staged rather than simultaneous: build and prove the reporting and dispatch platform on the first contract [A05], demonstrate the 95% fulfilment floor across at least one full quarter, then use that demonstrated track record, not a cold pitch, as the evidence base for approaching a second buyer from the remaining five named companies.

T29.5. The land-and-expand staging, inside the one contract and toward a second client

Stage What is proven Timing Tag
Land: electrify the existing fleet EV operations, charging, lease management work at SwiftKart's own demonstrated scale months 2 to 12 [M, T8]
Land: contract tranche 1 25 EVs, fulfilment and reporting proven at partial contract volume month 4 M
Land: contract tranche 2 and 3 Full 75-vehicle contract fleet live, 95% fulfilment floor tested at scale months 6 to 8 [M, C O03]
Expand: within the contract Volume ramps from about 70% of plateau in the first month of supply toward 100% months 8 to 12 A09, A10, A11
Expand: toward a second client Demonstrated track record (fulfilment, monthly emissions reports) used as the pitch basis by month 24, a goal M

This staging shows land-and-expand operating at two levels at once, inside the single contract's own tranche schedule, and across the funnel toward a possible second client; neither level assumes a vehicle or a client arrives before the stage before it is proven.

29.6 Ansoff matrix placement: market penetration with the existing base, market development toward the contract client

Applying the Ansoff matrix's existing/new market and existing/new product axes to SwiftKart's own growth choice: converting the existing 100 petrol bikes to leased EVs is market penetration, the lowest-risk Ansoff quadrant, selling the same delivery service to the same client relationships SwiftKart already serves, with a new vehicle technology rather than a new market or a new product [C B01, C B02]. Winning and fulfilling the anchor contract is market development, a new client relationship (the contract client is not named among SwiftKart's existing business in the case) reached with the same core delivery service SwiftKart already performs, not a new product line. Neither move is product development or diversification in the Ansoff sense: SwiftKart is not building a new type of service, only extending its existing delivery service to a new buyer and running it on a different vehicle technology for its existing buyers.

T29.6. Ansoff matrix placement for SwiftKart's two growth moves

Existing product (last-mile delivery service) New product
Existing market (current client base) Market penetration: convert 100 petrol bikes to leased EVs, same clients, same service, lower running cost [C D12, T2] not pursued
New market (the contract client) Market development: win the anchor contract, same delivery service, a new buyer relationship, 75 vehicles [C O01, C O02] not pursued

The recommended plan occupies only the two lowest-risk Ansoff quadrants, market penetration and market development, deliberately; it does not attempt product development (a new kind of logistics service) or diversification (a new product to a new market), which the research document's own frameworks table (ARGUMENT.md) names as a conscious scope choice, not an omission.

29.7 Client concentration: Shadowfax's 74% norm, and what it means for SwiftKart specifically

Section 29.4's table already places SwiftKart's post-award concentration, close to half of combined revenue from one contract, inside the comparable range Shadowfax discloses, about 74% from four named clients [RA35]. What this means for SwiftKart specifically is twofold. First, it means the single-contract dependence the anchor contract creates is not, on its own, evidence of an unusually risky growth plan; it is the industry-typical shape of a last-mile 3PL's revenue base once it wins a large e-commerce or quick-commerce client, confirmed at three orders of magnitude greater scale by Shadowfax's own disclosure. Second, it means the cost of losing that single relationship is real and quantified by a direct precedent: Meesho's own in-house logistics arm, Valmo, displaced a third-party 3PL partner's volume so fast that Meesho's Q3 FY26 losses widened roughly thirteen-fold, partly attributed to "a large 3PL partner" abruptly exiting the business [RA43, RA45]. For SwiftKart, the practical reading is the reverse risk, that the client, not SwiftKart, could choose to insource or re-tender the relationship, which is why the recommended plan's own risk register treats contract non-renewal and volume-ramp shortfall (R3, R5) as the two highest-impact items on its heat map, not treated here again in full since research section 21 carries the register itself.

29.8 How monthly emissions reporting and BRSR value-chain pressure open the door with these clients

Section 6 of this document (part-B) established that SEBI's BRSR Core framework, after its 28 March 2025 amendment, makes value-chain ESG disclosure voluntary rather than comply-or-explain for listed clients [RC55, RC56], and that none of Zomato's Hyperpure code, Swiggy's supplier code, or Flipkart's supplier standards excerpt carries an explicit EV-use or periodic-emissions-reporting clause for a logistics partner, when each document is read in full [RI32, RI33, RI35]. What this means concretely for SwiftKart's go-to-market motion is that the contract's own monthly emissions-reporting clause [C O05] is not a regulatory compliance demand being imposed on SwiftKart from above; it is the client's own operational choice to source data it can use for its own voluntary BRSR Core value-chain disclosure, once SwiftKart's contracted spend is large enough to cross the 2%-of-purchases individual-partner threshold the 2025 amendment sets [RC57]. A fleet operator that can already produce this data, built and proven on the existing fleet before contract volume arrives (research section 17.2's ₹13.0 lakh reporting and dispatch platform line), removes a real adoption friction for a listed buyer that would otherwise need to ask a new logistics partner to build this capability from a standing start. This is the door the emissions-reporting capability opens, not a formal requirement any of the six named buyers' own codes of conduct currently mandates.

T29.7. What the emissions-reporting capability removes as a go-to-market friction

Friction a new 3PL partner usually represents What SwiftKart's built-ahead capability removes Tag
No telematics or distance-tracking in place Reporting and dispatch platform built in month 2, ahead of contract award (research §17.2) [T9, A05]
No defined emission-factor methodology GHG Protocol Scope 3 Category 4 mapping and the six recurring data fields already defined (research §6.4, §6.7) [research §6.4, §6.7]
Client must wait for the partner to build reporting capability before requesting voluntary BRSR Core data Capability already proven on the existing fleet before the contract's first reporting cycle M

None of the three codes of conduct read in full for this lane, Hyperpure's, Swiggy's and Flipkart's excerpt, contains a binding EV-use or emissions-reporting clause for a logistics partner [RI32, RI33, RI35]; the door this section describes is a competitive-readiness advantage, not a contractual obligation SwiftKart is being forced to meet.

29.9 The second client by month 24 is a goal, not a forecast, and what would make it happen

The funnel's final stage, "+1, second client by month 24," is stated by the recommended plan itself as a goal, never a forecast [M]. No conversion rate, no probability of winning a second client, and no named second client are invented anywhere in this document or in the deck's funnel panel; the research base simply does not contain data that would support assigning a probability to winning a second contract among the five remaining named buyers, and the honest position is to say so rather than to manufacture a plausible-looking percentage. What would make the goal real, rather than aspirational, follows directly from sections 29.5 and 29.8 above: a full quarter of demonstrated 95% fulfilment on the anchor contract [C O03], at least two accepted monthly emissions reports built to the six data fields this document's section 6.7 derives, and a reporting and dispatch platform already proven, not newly built, at the point a second buyer is approached. These are the same three conditions research section 22's roadmap gates (G2, G3) test for the anchor contract itself, read here as the evidence a second buyer's own procurement team would plausibly ask for before signing, not as a SwiftKart-specific sales tactic invented for this section.

T29.8. What would convert the month-24 goal into a real second client, against what the plan already builds

Precondition a second buyer would plausibly test for Already built into the recommended plan, by when Tag
Demonstrated fulfilment at or above 95% Tested continuously from contract tranche 1 (month 4); gate G2 checks it at month 8 [C O03, M]
At least one full quarter of accepted monthly emissions reports Reporting platform live from month 2; first full quarter of contract operation by month 8 to 11 [T9, M]
EV-native fleet operations at demonstrated scale, not a pilot 175 vehicles, zero petrol, by month 12 (gate G3) [T8, M]
A reference relationship with at least one named large buyer The anchor contract itself, once awarded C O01

This table states preconditions, not a committed timeline or a named prospective second client; the research document does not assign a probability or a date to any individual precondition being met by a second buyer specifically, because no such data exists in the case brief or in any verified source opened for this lane.

What this section establishes, and what it does not

  • It establishes, with an independent source for every stage, the exact shape of the funnel on slide S5: six named buyers, five with a company-authored EV commitment, three with a 2030 100% target specifically, one anchor contract at 75 vehicles and ₹2.8 crore of potential annual revenue, and a second client by month 24 named explicitly as a goal.
  • It establishes the land-and-expand logic operating at two levels, the contract's own tranche schedule and the funnel's progression toward a second buyer, and places both growth moves on the Ansoff matrix, market penetration for the existing fleet and market development for the contract client.
  • It establishes that SwiftKart's post-award client concentration sits inside the comparable-operator norm Shadowfax discloses (74% from four clients), using Meesho's own abrupt 3PL-exit precedent as evidence of what the opposite risk, losing the relationship, has cost a comparable buyer in the past.
  • It establishes the regulatory and contractual mechanism, BRSR Core's voluntary value-chain layer, through which a built-ahead emissions-reporting capability becomes a go-to-market advantage with listed buyers, while stating plainly that none of the three codes of conduct read in full contains a binding clause requiring it.
  • It does not invent a conversion rate, a win probability, or a named second client anywhere in this section; the goal of a second client by month 24 is stated as a goal, with its preconditions named, not as a forecast with an implied probability.
  • It does not change the case's own contract terms [C O01] to [C O09] or any locked model number; this section explains the market context the anchor contract sits inside, without altering the contract itself.

30. Capital timing and payback: ₹87.9 L of the crore is out by month 8, and the deployed ₹94.2 L is earned back by month 13

Answer. The recommended plan deploys ₹87.9 L of the ₹1 crore by month 8 and ₹94.2 L by month 12, the point at which deployment stops entirely [M]. Cumulative contribution over the petrol baseline of ₹3.52 L a month [C D05, C D06, T2] first equals or exceeds cumulative deployment at month 13, ₹104.1 L of contribution against ₹94.2 L deployed, which is the model's own payback crossover [M]. If petrol sale proceeds are counted into cumulative earnings alongside contribution, the same crossover happens two months earlier, at month 11 [M]. A sources-and-uses view across both pools of cash totals ₹129.7 L, ₹100.0 L from the crore and ₹29.7 L from petrol resale [T17.4], and the working-capital line inside the crore, ₹44.5 L, is the direct arithmetic result of 57 verified receivable days applied to ₹23.4 L of monthly contract billing at plateau [A01, C O07]. A full subsidy stress-test shows that even stacking the Delhi EV Policy 2026 year-1 cap of ₹30,000 with PM E-DRIVE's ₹5,000 leaves a bought EV at ₹5,038 a month all-in, still above the ₹3,500 lease, and that ₹94,521 of subsidy, not ₹35,000, would be needed to flip the comparison [T13, M].

30.1 The monthly deployment table, M1 to M12, by use

The five non-reserve uses of the crore, contract working capital, the charging hub, lease deposits, the reporting and dispatch platform, and rider hiring and training, are drawn on different schedules across the first 12 months, read directly from the model's own monthly rows [M]. The reporting platform is a single ₹13.0 L build in month 2, ahead of the contract's own award [A05, A08]. The charging hub and lease deposits move together, in step with each wave and tranche of EVs arriving, months 2, 4, 6, 8 and 12 [M]. Rider costs move with both the existing-fleet waves and the contract tranches, months 2, 4, 6, 8 and 12 [A03, A04]. Contract working capital begins only once the contract itself earns revenue, month 4, and grows through month 10, the only one of the five lines still moving after month 8 [A01].

Figures are the model's own monthly row values for the five use categories, matching deck/values_ext.py's V.dep_series and V.dep_tot exactly [M]; small rounding differences between the per-category figures and the month total are a rounding artefact of presenting two-decimal L figures to one decimal, not a calculation error, and the model's own check confirms the five lines sum to ₹94.2 L undiscounted by month 12 [T17].

Reading the cumulative column directly answers the title's first number: ₹87.9 L of the crore is out by month 8, which is the model's own value used verbatim in the deck's in-chart annotation [M]. By month 12, cumulative deployment reaches ₹94.2 L and stops; no further draw happens in any of the remaining 12 months of the 24-month horizon, because all five non-reserve lines are, by this point, either fully spent (the charging hub, deposits, reporting platform, riders) or have reached their peak and begun running off (working capital, which the model shows essentially flat from month 9 as the contract's revenue ramp slows toward plateau).

30.2 Cumulative deployed against cumulative contribution over the petrol baseline, months 1 to 24

The payback question asked by this section's title is answered by comparing two running totals: cumulative capital deployed from the crore (T30.1's last column, extended to month 24, where it stays flat at ₹94.2 L) against cumulative contribution earned above the petrol baseline SwiftKart would otherwise have kept, ₹3.52 L a month at today's 85% utilisation [C D05, C D06, C D08, T2]. The baseline is not zero; it is what the existing fleet already earns without the plan, so the comparison measures the plan's own incremental contribution, not the fleet's total contribution, against the capital the plan itself commits.

T30.2. Cumulative deployed against cumulative contribution over the petrol baseline, months 1 to 24, ₹ L

Month Cumulative deployed Cumulative contribution over baseline Gap, contribution minus deployed
M1 0.0 0.0 0.0
M2 22.9 2.5 −20.4
M4 46.5 9.2 −37.3

Cumulative contribution over the baseline is computed month by month as that month's recommended-plan contribution minus the ₹3.52 L petrol baseline, summed from month 1, matching the method deck/values_ext.py uses to build V.pb_inv and V.pb_earn for the payback crossover chart on S4 [M]. The gap column is this document's own addition, to show the crossover happening between month 12 and month 13 rather than asserting it without the arithmetic.

The gap column makes the crossover visible without rounding ambiguity: at month 12, the plan has deployed ₹3.7 L more than it has earned back; at month 13, the plan has earned ₹9.9 L more than it has deployed. The crossover therefore falls inside month 13, which the model identifies as the first month at which cumulative contribution over the baseline equals or exceeds cumulative deployment [M]. This is the method shown in full, not merely asserted: the deployed total stops moving after month 12 (T30.1), while the earned total keeps growing every month, because the contract's own revenue ramp continues through month 10 and the full fleet keeps earning its plateau contribution of ₹17.2 L a month from month 12 onward [T7].

30.3 The payback crossover at month 13, and the earlier month 11 crossover if petrol sale proceeds are counted in

Section 30.2's ₹94.2 L deployed figure counts only the five non-reserve uses of the crore itself; it does not count the ₹29.7 L of petrol sale proceeds the plan separately generates by selling retired petrol bikes in three waves, 50 in month 2, 40 in month 4, the last 10 in month 12 [T17.3]. If those proceeds are added to the cumulative-earned side of the comparison, in the same months they actually land, cumulative earnings cross cumulative deployment two months earlier, at month 11, not month 13 [M]. This is not a different, more favourable payback claim replacing the first one; it is the same arithmetic answering a slightly different question, whether petrol resale cash counts as part of what the plan has earned back. The research document reports both months rather than choosing the more favourable one silently, because the choice of which cash flow counts toward payback is a modelling convention, not a fact with one right answer.

T30.3. Payback crossover, with and without petrol sale proceeds counted into cumulative earnings, ₹ L

Month Cumulative deployed Cumulative earned, contribution only Cumulative earned, contribution plus petrol sales Crossover without sales Crossover with sales
M10 92.3 63.7 90.7 no no
M11 92.3 76.8 103.8 no yes, 103.8 at or above 92.3
M12 94.2 90.5 120.2 no yes
M13 94.2 104.1 133.8 yes, 104.1 at or above 94.2 yes

The "with sales" column adds each month's petrol sale proceeds, ₹15.0 L in month 2, ₹12.0 L in month 4, ₹2.7 L in month 12 [T17.3], to that month's contribution-over-baseline figure before cumulating; the crossover test is the same in both columns, cumulative earned at or above cumulative deployed. Both months are reported in the research document and in this section; the deck's own payback panel uses month 13, the more conservative of the two, as the headline figure [M].

Why the recommended plan's own documentation, the deck and this section's own title, leads with month 13 rather than the earlier month 11: petrol sale proceeds are a one-time, finite pool of cash, not a recurring earning the plan generates every month going forward, and counting them into the ongoing payback measure would understate how much of the plan's return comes from its actual, sustained operating contribution rather than from liquidating an asset it no longer needs. Month 11 is reported here as the honest alternative reading, not hidden, but month 13 is the figure this document and the deck both use as the primary claim.

30.4 Sources and uses, reconciled across both pools of cash, ₹129.7 L total

Putting the crore and the petrol sale proceeds together gives the full capital base the plan draws on across 24 months: ₹100.0 L from the crore itself [C D09, C B07] plus ₹29.7 L of petrol sale proceeds [T17.3], a total of ₹129.7 L. The uses side carries the five non-reserve lines, ₹94.1 L, the ₹5.8 L reserve, and a balancing figure, ₹29.8 L, that is not a named budget line but the amount carried forward into the plan's ongoing cash account as contribution and sale proceeds accumulate month over month.

Sources ₹ L Uses ₹ L

Figures match deck/values_ext.py's V.su_total, V.su_src and V.su_use exactly, and the "carried into ongoing cash account" row is the same balancing figure research section 17.4 derives; it is the reason the model's own cash column never dips below ₹101.6 L in the base case despite the capital-intensive early months, since petrol sale proceeds arrive in the same months as the heaviest spend [T7].

30.5 The working-capital formula, shown in full

Contract working capital, the largest single line at ₹44.5 L, follows directly from the contract's own full-capacity annual revenue, ₹2.8 Cr [C O07], divided by 12 to give the monthly plateau billing figure: ₹2,80,00,000 divided by 12 is ₹23,33,333, which rounds to ₹23.3 L a month, close to the ₹23.4 L figure the deck's own panel cites once the case's own 75-vehicle, 30-delivery, 26-day, ₹40 figures are run through directly: 75 times 30 times 26 times ₹40 equals ₹23,40,000 a month [C O02, C D02, C D03, C D04]. The working-capital formula itself is the verified 57-day receivable period [A01] applied to that monthly billing rate, divided by 30 to convert the day-count into a fraction of a month, then multiplied by the monthly billing figure: 57 divided by 30 is 1.9, and 1.9 times ₹23,40,000 is ₹44,46,000, which rounds to the model's ₹44.5 L [T9]. The model's own figure is computed against the contract's ramping monthly revenue through months 4 to 10, not the flat plateau figure used in this illustrative calculation, which is why the exact modelled figure and this simplified formula agree to within rounding rather than matching to the rupee; the formula is shown here to demonstrate the method is reproducible from the case's own stated inputs, not to claim it is the literal line-by-line calculation the model runs internally.

T30.5. The working-capital formula, step by step

Step Calculation Result
Monthly contract billing at plateau 75 times 30 times 26 times ₹40 ₹23,40,000, or ₹23.4 L
Receivable period as a fraction of a month 57 days divided by 30 days a month 1.9 months
Working capital required 1.9 times ₹23,40,000 ₹44,46,000, or ₹44.5 L

The model's own T9 figure, ₹44.5 L, is computed against the contract's actual month-by-month revenue ramp rather than the flat plateau used in this illustrative three-step calculation, so the two are expected to agree closely rather than exactly; both are reported, and the difference is a modelling refinement, not an inconsistency between two sources [A01, T9, C O07].

30.6 The subsidy stress-test: ₹35,000 stacked, still short of flipping the lease-versus-buy comparison

A bought EV's full monthly cost, before any subsidy, is ₹5,684 all-in: ₹2,843 of capital recovery at 11% over 48 months, ₹258 of charging share, minus a ₹417 resale credit, plus ₹3,000 of running cost [T13, M]. Two live subsidy schemes could, in principle, reduce the effective capital cost: the Delhi EV Policy 2026's year-1 incentive, capped at ₹30,000 a vehicle, and PM E-DRIVE's e-2W subsidy, currently ₹5,000 a vehicle, unchanged since FY 2025-26 [RE29, RE03]. Stacking both gives a combined subsidy of ₹35,000 a vehicle, which this document's own model recomputation shows reduces the bought EV's all-in monthly cost from ₹5,684 to ₹5,038, a reduction of ₹646 a month [M]. Even at this combined subsidy level, the bought EV's all-in cost remains above the ₹3,500 lease by ₹1,538 a month, meaning the subsidy stress-test does not flip the lease-versus-buy comparison, and the recommendation to lease rather than buy holds under the maximum currently available stacked subsidy.

T30.6. The subsidy stress-test, step by step

Subsidy scenario Subsidy per EV Bought EV all-in monthly cost Against the ₹3,500 lease Tag
No subsidy ₹0 ₹5,684 ₹2,184 above the lease T13
Delhi EV Policy 2026 year-1 cap only ₹30,000 not separately modelled, see combined figure below RE29
PM E-DRIVE only ₹5,000 not separately modelled, see combined figure below RE03
Delhi EV Policy 2026 plus PM E-DRIVE, stacked ₹35,000 ₹5,038 ₹1,538 above the lease M
Subsidy required to flip the comparison ₹94,521 ₹3,500 at parity T13

The ₹94,521 switch point is the model's own T13 output, the subsidy level at which a bought EV's all-in monthly cost falls to exactly the ₹3,500 lease rate; the currently available ₹35,000 stacked subsidy is about 37% of the way to that switch point, not close to flipping it, which is also one of the plan's own kill criteria, ARGUMENT.md: the plan would be reconsidered only if a subsidy of ₹90,000 or more per purchased EV became available, and none currently does.

The practical reading of this stress-test is that the recommendation does not depend on subsidy policy remaining exactly as it is today; even a further, currently unannounced doubling of the stacked subsidy, to roughly ₹70,000, would still leave the bought EV above the lease rate, since the required figure to reach parity is ₹94,521, nearly two and a half times the current combined scheme. This is the honest reading of the subsidy question: the lease-versus-buy result in this document is robust to policy at its current, and even at a materially more generous, level, not contingent on subsidies holding at exactly today's value.
